title: 50 Ways to Leave Your Lover
description: Paul Simon turns a breakup into a rhyming game, riding Steve Gadd's famous drum groove to his only solo No. 1.

pops.text: That slinky drum groove is Steve Gadd's — a military-style pattern he cooked up in the studio that drummers still study like scripture.
Simon wrote this in the aftermath of his divorce from his first wife, Peggy Harper. Therapy, but make it rhyme.
Count the exits in the chorus: Jack, Stan, Roy, Gus and Lee. That's five ways — the other 45 are left as homework.
The parent album, Still Crazy After All These Years, won the Grammy for Album of the Year.
Those lush backing vocals come from Patti Austin, Valerie Simpson and Phoebe Snow — an all-star choir for a kiss-off.
Phil Ramone co-produced, recording Simon and a crack band of New York session aces live and loose.
Gadd's hi-hat and snare figure was so distinctive that he later demonstrated it in drum clinics around the world.
Released as a single in December 1975, it climbed to No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 in February 1976 and stayed three weeks.
It's still Simon's only No. 1 as a solo artist. Fifty ways, one chart-topper.

title: 100 Days, 100 Nights
description: Sharon Jones and the Dap-Kings bottle 1967 in 2007 — a retro-soul title track shot on $50 TV cameras.

pops.text: This video was shot on two vintage TV cameras director Adam Elias Buncher bought on eBay for $50 each. The grain is real.
Jones was 51 when this album arrived. Before music paid, she worked as a corrections officer and an armored-car guard.
She didn't release her first album until she was 40 — labels had told her she was too old, too short, not the look. Wrong on all counts.
The Dap-Kings record the old way at Daptone's Brooklyn studio: analog tape, vintage gear, no computers in the chain.
Between Sharon sessions, the Dap-Kings served as the house band behind Amy Winehouse's Back to Black.
Producer and bassist Gabriel Roth, aka Bosco Mann, built Daptone Records into soul's great revivalist label.
The lyric is a sentence and a promise: a hundred days and nights of proving love before she'll trust it.
Critics heard this title track as the soul revival's mission statement — 2007 sounding proudly like 1967.
Fans called Jones the female James Brown. She died in 2016, and this clip shows exactly why the title fit.

title: All Night Long (All Night)
description: Lionel Richie's Caribbean-flavored street party topped every chart in sight and turned 'all night long' into a permanent RSVP.

pops.text: Richie wanted a party with a Caribbean breeze — calypso rhythms, island percussion and a chorus built for street parades.
Those 'African' chant lines? Richie has admitted he improvised them — joyful gibberish he invented on the spot in the studio.
The video was directed by Bob Rafelson, co-creator of The Monkees and director of Five Easy Pieces. Yes, that Bob Rafelson.
It's from Can't Slow Down, which won the Grammy for Album of the Year and went Diamond in the US.
The single spent four weeks at No. 1 on the Hot 100 in the fall of 1983.
It didn't just top the pop chart — it hit No. 1 on the R&B and adult contemporary charts too.
Richie performed it at the closing ceremony of the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics, beamed to a global TV audience.
The street-party video, packed with dancers of every background, was Richie's vision of one world, one fiesta.
Four decades on, it's still the song wedding DJs reach for when the floor needs saving.

title: Always on My Mind
description: Pet Shop Boys feed an Elvis weeper through a synth and land the UK's Christmas No. 1 of 1987.

pops.text: The song was written by Johnny Christopher, Mark James and Wayne Carson, and first became a hit for Brenda Lee in 1972.
Elvis Presley recorded it in 1972, weeks after separating from Priscilla — you can hear it in his version.
Willie Nelson's 1982 take won three Grammys. The Pet Shop Boys' homework was intimidating.
Neil Tennant and Chris Lowe first performed it on Love Me Tender, an ITV tribute marking ten years since Elvis's death.
The TV performance went down so well that demand forced a single release. It was never the original plan.
It spent four weeks at UK No. 1 and took the coveted Christmas No. 1 spot for 1987.
The Pogues and Kirsty MacColl's Fairytale of New York was the record it held off at No. 2 that Christmas.
This video is an excerpt from the duo's surreal film It Couldn't Happen Here — the passenger is veteran actor Joss Ackland.
In America it reached No. 4 in 1988, proving a deadpan synth cover could out-swoon the originals.

title: Better Be Good to Me
description: Tina Turner delivers an ultimatum in leopard-print heels on the comeback album that relaunched her as a solo superstar.

pops.text: The song was written by Holly Knight, Nicky Chinn and Mike Chapman — a hit factory trio of the era.
Knight's own band, Spider, recorded it first in 1981. Tina's version is the one that drew blood.
It's from Private Dancer, the album that turned Turner, at 44, into the comeback story of the decade.
The video keeps it simple: Tina, a band, black leather and leopard-print heels. Charisma does the rest.
Director Brian Grant shot it as a straight performance — no plot needed when the singer owns every frame.
Fans heard the lyric as autobiography: a woman who'd left a controlling man now setting the terms. Turner let them.
The single reached No. 5 on the Billboard Hot 100 in the fall of 1984.
Turner won the Grammy for Best Female Rock Vocal Performance for this track — one of four Grammys she took home that year.
Private Dancer went on to sell over ten million copies worldwide. The ultimatum worked.

title: Brandy (You're a Fine Girl)
description: A harbor barmaid, a sailor married to the sea, and one perfect week at No. 1 for a band from Rutgers.

pops.text: Guitarist Elliot Lurie wrote it, sang it, and gave pop one of its great story songs: a barmaid, a sailor, a locket.
Looking Glass formed at Rutgers University in New Jersey and named themselves after Lewis Carroll's mirror world.
A Washington, D.C. promotion man pushed a test pressing to local radio, and the song broke out of the capital first.
It reached No. 1 on the Hot 100 in August 1972, holding the top for one week.
Legend claimed Brandy was based on Mary Ellis, a real New Jersey spinster. Lurie himself has debunked the story.
Barry Manilow's hit 'Mandy' was originally titled 'Brandy' too — it was renamed partly to avoid confusion with this record.
The band's follow-up, Jimmy Loves Mary-Anne, scraped the Top 40, but Brandy remains their defining three minutes.
In 2017, Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 built a key scene around the song — Ego calls it one of Earth's greatest compositions.
There was no video in 1972; this official animated clip was created decades later for the streaming era.

title: Caught Up in You
description: Jacksonville's 38 Special polish Southern rock into pure pop gold with help from the man who wrote Eye of the Tiger.

pops.text: Don Barnes sings lead — and check the credits: Survivor's Jim Peterik co-wrote this with Barnes and Jeff Carlisi.
Peterik had a busy 1982: the same year, his band Survivor took Eye of the Tiger to No. 1.
It's from Special Forces, the album that completed 38 Special's pivot from Southern boogie to arena-ready pop-rock.
The band hailed from Jacksonville, Florida — Donnie Van Zant, co-frontman here, is the younger brother of Lynyrd Skynyrd's Ronnie.
The video cuts between the band and a barroom storyline, with model and actress Shari Shattuck as the woman in pink.
This became the group's first No. 1 on Billboard's rock chart.
On the Hot 100 it peaked at No. 10 — their biggest pop hit alongside Hold On Loosely's groundwork.
Two drummers powered the classic lineup's live sound, a Southern rock tradition borrowed from the Allmans' playbook.
Special Forces went platinum, and this chorus has been a classic-rock radio fixture ever since.

title: Don't Stop 'Til You Get Enough
description: Michael Jackson, newly unleashed with Quincy Jones, writes his own coronation anthem — falsetto, giggle and all.

pops.text: Michael wrote this one himself, words and music — his declaration of independence from the Jackson 5 machinery.
The home demo was cut in the family studio with brother Randy banging percussion. The groove survived to the master.
Producer Quincy Jones's first collaboration with Jackson. Off the Wall was the test run for Thriller.
That breathy intro — the giggle, the shriek — was Jackson finding the vocal tics that would define a decade.
Brothers Johnson bassist Louis Johnson and keyboardist Greg Phillinganes anchor the funkiest rhythm section money could hire.
Released in July 1979, it hit No. 1 on the Hot 100 that October and also topped the soul chart.
It earned Jackson his first Grammy, Best Male R&B Vocal Performance, at the 1980 ceremony.
The video, directed by Nick Saxton, triples Michael via early chroma-key tricks — a tux, a smile and pure footwork.
Off the Wall sold in the tens of millions and rewrote what a former child star could become.

title: Don't You Want Me
description: A cocktail-bar waitress, a svengali and a photo-story plot: the synth-pop duet that ruled Christmas 1981 and America in '82.

pops.text: Philip Oakey spotted singers Susan Sulley and Joanne Catherall dancing in a Sheffield nightclub — they were schoolgirls of 17 and 18.
Oakey has said the lyric was inspired by a photo-story in a teen magazine: boy makes girl a star, girl walks away.
That opening line — 'You were working as a waitress in a cocktail bar' — is one of pop's great first sentences.
Producer Martin Rushent built the sound at his Genetic Studios; the parent album is Dare.
Oakey thought this was the weakest track on the album and fought its release as a single. History overruled him.
It became the UK's Christmas No. 1 in 1981 and the year's best-selling British single.
Director Steve Barron shot the video on film with a movie-set concept: a video within a video, very 1981.
In July 1982 it topped the US Hot 100, helping kick off the Second British Invasion of synth acts.
Sulley and Catherall needed their parents' permission to tour. The homework could wait; pop history couldn't.

title: Down Under
description: A Vegemite sandwich, a fried-out Kombi and the flute riff that made Australia the center of the pop universe.

pops.text: Colin Hay and Ron Strykert wrote it in Melbourne; a slower early version first appeared as a B-side on an indie single in 1979.
That flute riff is Greg Ham's. Decades later an Australian court ruled part of it echoed the children's song Kookaburra.
Yes, that's a real lyric: a six-foot-four man in Brussels serves the narrator a Vegemite sandwich.
'Chunder' is Aussie slang for vomiting — 'where beer does flow and men chunder' is not a compliment to the beer.
The video sends the band through the desert in a Kombi van, acting out the song's travelogue frame by frame.
Hay was born in Scotland and emigrated to Australia as a teenager — the song is an immigrant's love letter to his new home.
In early 1983 it spent four weeks at No. 1 in the US, and topped the UK chart too.
Men at Work became the first Australian act to hold the No. 1 single and No. 1 album in America at the same time.
Business as Usual sat atop the US album chart for 15 weeks. Not bad for five blokes from down under.

title: Footloose
description: Kenny Loggins, the king of the 80s soundtrack, soundtracks a town that banned dancing — and dares you to sit still.

pops.text: The film was loosely inspired by Elmore City, Oklahoma, where dancing had been banned for nearly a century until local teens challenged it in 1980.
Screenwriter Dean Pitchford wrote the lyrics to every song in the film; Loggins co-wrote this title track with him.
By 1984 Loggins was Hollywood's go-to voice: I'm Alright for Caddyshack before this, Danger Zone for Top Gun after.
The single spent three weeks at No. 1 on the Hot 100 in the spring of 1984.
The Footloose soundtrack album climbed to No. 1 — briefly knocking Michael Jackson's Thriller off the top.
Kevin Bacon's warehouse dance was assisted by doubles, including a gymnast and a dance stand-in, for the wildest moves.
The song was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Original Song.
This video is basically the movie in miniature: dancing feet, prom lights and a town cutting loose.
Loggins has said audiences still treat the opening drum hits like a starting pistol. He's not wrong.

title: Got to Give It Up
description: Marvin Gaye, ordered to make a disco record, throws a party in the studio instead — and tops three charts at once.

pops.text: Motown wanted a disco hit. Gaye, no disco fan, answered with a loose, laughing parody that became the real thing.
Hear the chatter under the groove? Gaye filled his Marvin's Room studio with friends and family and recorded the party.
His brother Frankie and his wife Janis are among the voices in the room — it's a family gathering with a backbeat.
The full version runs nearly twelve minutes and was tucked onto Live at the London Palladium — a studio track hiding on a live album.
This single edit, Part 1, topped the Hot 100, the R&B chart and the dance chart simultaneously in 1977.
Gaye plays much of the track himself and produced the session with engineer Art Stewart.
Michael Jackson studied this record closely — its floating groove is all over Off the Wall two years later.
In 2015, a jury ruled that Robin Thicke's Blurred Lines infringed this song, awarding Gaye's estate millions.
Aaliyah covered it in 1996 with Slick Rick. The party, apparently, never really ends.

title: Hold On Loosely
description: Relationship advice you can shout along to — hold on loosely, but don't let go — from the album that broke 38 Special wide open.

pops.text: The title came out of a conversation between Don Barnes and co-writer Jim Peterik about a relationship — 'hold on loosely, but don't let go' was the hook, written in about ninety minutes.
Peterik, of Survivor and the Ides of March, became the band's secret weapon, co-writing this and Caught Up in You.
This live performance clip was the song's official video — and it was the 13th video MTV played on its first day, August 1, 1981.
It's from Wild-Eyed Southern Boys, the band's first platinum album.
Barnes sings lead and plays guitar; co-frontman Donnie Van Zant is the other voice of the classic lineup.
The lyric is a fortune cookie that works: grip too tight and you lose her, too loose and she's gone.
On the Hot 100 it peaked at No. 27, but on rock radio it was inescapable — and still is.
The arrangement is the pivot point where Southern rock learned pop choruses without losing the guitars.
Forty-plus years of touring later, this is the song the whole room sings back word for word.

title: It's My Life
description: Mark Hollis refuses to lip-sync — literally — in a synth-pop hit with a wildlife film where its video should be.

pops.text: Mark Hollis and Tim Friese-Greene wrote it; that pulsing synth riff and fretless-feel bass line do the rest.
The first video, directed by Tim Pope, is almost entirely wildlife documentary footage, with Hollis standing silently in London Zoo.
It was a deliberate protest against lip-syncing. EMI was not amused and demanded a normal video.
So the band delivered this second version, lip-syncing as badly and theatrically as possible. Compliance, weaponized.
First time around it was a modest hit in the US and bigger in continental Europe than at home in Britain.
A 1990 reissue finally took it into the UK Top 20, peaking at No. 13.
No Doubt's 2003 cover went further in America, reaching the US Top 10 and introducing the song to a new generation.
Talk Talk soon abandoned pop stardom entirely, inventing post-rock on Spirit of Eden and Laughing Stock.
Hollis retired from music in the late 90s and died in 2019 — this chorus remains his loudest goodbye.

title: It's Not Unusual
description: A demo meant for Sandie Shaw becomes a Welsh coal-country kid's UK No. 1 — with a future Elton John at the session piano.

pops.text: Writers Les Reed and Gordon Mills intended this for Sandie Shaw. Jones cut the demo — and Shaw told him to release it himself.
It was recorded in November 1964 at Decca Studios in London, in a single day's session.
Among the session players: a young Reg Dwight on piano duties — a few years before he renamed himself Elton John.
Guitar credit is a pub argument: Jimmy Page's sessionography lists the date, but arranger Les Reed maintained the guitarist was Joe Moretti.
The BBC initially refused to play it, wary of Jones's sexy image. Pirate radio ships broke it instead.
It hit No. 1 in the UK in 1965 and No. 10 in America — his first US hit, sealed with three Ed Sullivan Show performances.
The song became the theme of his TV variety series This Is Tom Jones at the end of the decade.
Thirty years later, Alfonso Ribeiro's Carlton dance on The Fresh Prince of Bel-Air made it a 90s anthem all over again.
Jones was 24, from Pontypridd, Wales, and on his second single. The voice did the rest.

title: Lido Shuffle
description: Boz Scaggs and the future members of Toto shuffle a drifter named Lido toward one last score.

pops.text: Scaggs co-wrote it with keyboardist David Paich — remember that name; his bandmates here are about to become Toto.
The Silk Degrees sessions at Davlen Sound in Hollywood used Paich, drummer Jeff Porcaro and bassist David Hungate — three-fifths of Toto.
Lido is a drifter who 'missed the boat that day he left the shack' and spends the song chasing one more payday.
The groove is a shuffle with a New Orleans strut smuggled into a California studio.
Silk Degrees peaked at No. 2 in the US and turned Scaggs from critics' favorite into a platinum act.
Released as a single in 1977, Lido Shuffle climbed to No. 11 on the Hot 100.
Album-mate Lowdown won the Grammy for Best R&B Song — the smoothest one-two punch of 1976.
Scaggs had paid dues in the Steve Miller Band in the 60s; the two were schoolmates back in Texas.
Silk Degrees is now filed under yacht rock royalty. Lido, presumably, is still waiting on that boat.

title: The Look of Love
description: Trevor Horn's orchestral pop machine, Martin Fry's gold suit, and a breakup turned into the most glamorous single of 1982.

pops.text: Producer Trevor Horn built this like a film score — real orchestra, arranged by a young Anne Dudley, over a dance groove.
Martin Fry wrote the Lexicon of Love lyrics out of a real breakup. Heartbreak, but make it couture.
The single sprawls across four parts on its various releases — Part One is the hit; Parts Two through Four get dubby and strange.
It reached No. 4 in the UK, the band's biggest British hit, and No. 18 in the US while topping the American dance chart.
The video restages an Edwardian park scene; producer Trevor Horn and journalist Paul Morley both cameo.
Horn met Morley at this very video shoot — a meeting that led directly to ZTT Records and Frankie Goes to Hollywood.
Fry's gold lamé suit in the video became his trademark — he still wears it for the encore, decades later.
Parent album The Lexicon of Love hit UK No. 1 and routinely lands on greatest-albums-ever lists.
Horn called ABC's brief 'a record that sounds like it cost a million pounds.' It sounds like it.

title: Move by Yourself
description: Pro surfer turned soul man Donavon Frankenreiter trades beach-folk for a funky full band on his second album's title track.

pops.text: Before the records, Frankenreiter was a professional surfer, sponsored through his teens and twenties.
He started on guitar at 16 — a story he tells involves a guitar left behind at the house he was renting in San Clemente.
His close friend Jack Johnson gave him his break; Johnson's Brushfire label released Donavon's debut.
This is the title track of his second album, released in June 2006 on Lost Highway Records.
Where the debut was barefoot folk, this album plugs in: a full band, Hammond organ and a 70s soul-funk strut.
Album-mate Lovely Day slipped into the Snakes on a Plane soundtrack the same summer.
The lyric is a gentle ultimatum — nobody's dragging you to happiness; you've got to move by yourself.
He recorded it with his touring band rather than session ringers, keeping the groove loose and live.
Two decades on he still tours the surf towns he grew up playing — board in the van, just in case.

title: The Promise
description: Three Mancunians promise to be there — a piano-led synth ballad that flopped at home, conquered America late, and closed Napoleon Dynamite.

pops.text: The trio — Clive Farrington, Michael Floreale and Andrew Mann — wrote it together in Manchester.
Yes, the band name is the proverb: when in Rome, do as the Romans do.
Released in Britain in 1987, it barely troubled the UK chart. America would take two years to catch up.
That stately piano line makes it a synth-pop oddity — more hymn than club track, which is exactly why it lasted.
In 1989 it finally peaked at No. 11 on the Billboard Hot 100, a slow-burn sleeper hit.
Farrington's choirboy tenor against the promise lyric made it a wedding-dance staple for a generation.
In 2004, Napoleon Dynamite ended with this song over the tetherball scene, handing it to a whole new audience.
The band later split into two rival touring lineups using the same name — the promise got complicated.
One-hit wonder on paper; in practice, one of the most durable love songs of the synth era.

title: Promises, Promises
description: Pete Byrne sings from a jail cell about promises nobody kept — and the US remix quietly features a young Madonna.

pops.text: Naked Eyes were Pete Byrne and Rob Fisher, a duo from Bath, England, armed with synthesizers and matching cheekbones.
Byrne and Fisher wrote it; the hook is an accusation — 'You made me promises, promises, knowing I'd believe.'
For the American single, remixer Jellybean Benitez reworked it — and his then-girlfriend Madonna added backing vocals.
Her voice is on the US remix only, not the album version. She was months away from her own debut album.
The video, directed by Simon Milne, puts Byrne in a striped prison uniform behind bars — heartbreak as incarceration.
It reached No. 11 on the Billboard Hot 100 in the fall of 1983.
The duo's bigger US hit was a cover: Always Something There to Remind Me, the Bacharach and David standard.
Fisher later formed Climie Fisher and co-wrote Love Changes (Everything). The man knew a chorus.
Rob Fisher died in 1999. Byrne has since revived Naked Eyes on tour, promises kept this time.

title: Rock This Town
description: Three kids from Long Island in creepers and pompadours make 1956 sound like the future, with Dave Edmunds producing.

pops.text: Brian Setzer wrote it, and plays guitar like the building's on fire — because in this song, it basically is.
Producer Dave Edmunds, rockabilly's Welsh high priest, captured the trio mostly live and very loud.
The band are just three: Setzer, Lee Rocker slapping an upright bass, and Slim Jim Phantom standing up at a stripped-down drum kit.
They came from Massapequa, Long Island — but America ignored them first, so they moved to London and broke in Britain.
Released as a UK single in 1981 from their debut album; America caught up via the Built for Speed compilation in 1982.
In the US it stormed to No. 9 on the Hot 100 — a pompadour in the age of synth-pop.
The Rock and Roll Hall of Fame counts it among the songs that shaped rock and roll.
Setzer was barely into his twenties and already playing like Eddie Cochran's heir — because somebody had to.
The Cats sparked a full rockabilly revival: quiffs, creepers and upright basses, back in the charts.

title: Run to You
description: Blue Öyster Cult passed on it; Bryan Adams kept the first take, made his guitar the other woman, and launched Reckless.

pops.text: Adams and Jim Vallance wrote it on January 10, 1983 — and first offered it to Blue Öyster Cult, who turned it down.
It became the last song completed for Reckless and the album's lead single, released in October 1984.
Adams has said the guitar intro you hear is the very first take from the session. Some songs arrive finished.
The lyric is a confession of infidelity — but in the video, the 'other woman' is revealed to be his guitar.
Director Steve Barron, fresh off Billie Jean, shot it in London and Los Angeles with actress Lysette Anthony.
The video earned five MTV Video Music Award nominations in 1985 — more than any other Adams clip.
It topped Billboard's rock chart and reached No. 6 on the Hot 100, his biggest US hit to that point.
Reckless itself was released on Adams's 25th birthday and went on to sell in the millions worldwide.
Grand Theft Auto: Vice City put it on Flash FM, where it has been soundtracking virtual joyrides since 2002.

title: Sign Your Name
description: Terence Trent D'Arby — now Sananda Maitreya — croons a doo-wop-kissed vow that hit No. 1 in Ireland and No. 4 in America.

pops.text: He released this as Terence Trent D'Arby, the name the world met him under in 1987; he legally became Sananda Maitreya in 2001.
He says the new name came to him in a series of dreams — the old one, he felt, had died with his first career chapter.
The song was released as a single on December 28, 1987, from his blockbuster debut Introducing the Hardline.
Those 'bop shoo wop' backing vocals are pure doo-wop, smuggled into a state-of-the-art 80s soul production.
The video, directed by Vaughan Arnell and premiered in January 1988, features model Kelly Brennan.
A remix by dub legend Lee 'Scratch' Perry exists — one of pop's more unlikely and delightful credits.
It hit No. 1 in Ireland, No. 2 in the UK and No. 4 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1988.
The debut album sold millions and won him a Grammy for Best Male R&B Vocal Performance.
Sheryl Crow covered this in 2010, with Justin Timberlake slipping into the backing vocals.

title: Smooth Criminal
description: Michael Jackson in full gangster-movie mode, asking after Annie over one of the tightest grooves on Bad.

pops.text: Jackson wrote this himself, and it became the centerpiece of his 1988 film Moonwalker, where this full-length video first appeared.
The scene is a 1930s-style speakeasy, with Jackson in a white suit and fedora modeled on classic Hollywood tough guys — and Fred Astaire.
That impossible forward lean? No camera trick. Jackson co-invented a patented shoe that locked into pegs on the stage floor.
The lean was first done in this video using wires, then re-engineered with the special shoes so he could pull it off live on tour.
"Annie, are you OK?" echoes the phrase rescuers are taught to say to Resusci Annie, the CPR training dummy — Jackson had taken a CPR course.
Quincy Jones produced the track for the album Bad, where it sat alongside five number-one singles, a Billboard record at the time.
As a single it climbed to number 7 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1988, even without a conventional standalone video release at first.
The sped-up heartbeat and heavy breathing under the intro came from Jackson's own heartbeat, recorded and processed in the studio.
Alien Ant Farm's 2001 cover took the song back up the charts, hitting number 1 on Billboard's Modern Rock Tracks list.

title: Steppin' Out
description: Joe Jackson dresses up for a neon New York night in this sleek, piano-driven slice of 1982 pop.

pops.text: This was Jackson's love letter to New York nightlife, written after he moved to the city and fell for its after-dark energy.
It's from Night and Day, an album named in tribute to Cole Porter, and the record is famous for having no guitars on it at all.
The whole track rides on piano, bass, drums and percussion — that bouncing bassline is Graham Maby, Jackson's longtime bassist.
Director Steve Barron shot the video in and around a New York hotel, cutting Jackson's performance against a couple's night out.
Barron would soon become an MTV fixture, directing era-defining clips for Michael Jackson, a-ha and Dire Straits.
The single reached number 6 on the Billboard Hot 100, still the biggest American hit of Jackson's career.
It earned a Grammy nomination for Record of the Year, and Night and Day landed on best-of-the-decade lists for years afterward.
Jackson, a classically trained musician, built the song's sparkle from Latin-tinged percussion and a rolling, almost music-box piano figure.
Four decades on, that piano riff remains a favorite sample-and-cover target, and the song is a staple of 80s radio worldwide.

title: Supernova
description: Ray LaMontagne plugs in and goes psychedelic, trading hushed folk for a sun-warmed 60s rock shimmer.

pops.text: This was the title track and lead single from LaMontagne's fifth studio album, released in 2014.
The album was produced by Dan Auerbach of The Black Keys, a pairing that pushed LaMontagne toward a fuller band sound.
Sessions took place at Auerbach's Easy Eye Sound studio in Nashville, a room built for vintage tones and live takes.
After years of whisper-quiet folk records, the psychedelic 60s and 70s rock shimmer here was a deliberate left turn.
LaMontagne has said the album's songs arrived quickly, written in a burst rather than labored over for years.
The kaleidoscopic official video matches the brief — all saturated color and trippy overlays instead of a storyline.
Critics singled out the title track as the album's most immediate song, and it became a fixture of adult-alternative radio.
Supernova the album debuted in the top 3 of the Billboard 200, his strongest chart showing up to that point.
Live, the song anchors the electric half of his shows — a long way from the one-microphone folk clubs where he started.

title: Sweet Dreams (Are Made of This)
description: Annie Lennox, orange-haired and ice-cool, turns a cheap synth riff into synth-pop's defining statement.

pops.text: Eurythmics recorded this in a cramped attic studio in north London, working with gear bought through a bank loan they talked a manager into approving.
The famous synth riff was almost an accident — Dave Stewart stumbled onto the sequence while experimenting, and Annie Lennox jumped up to sing over it.
Lennox wrote the lyric in a bleak mood after a fight and a failing record deal; the sweet part is strictly ironic.
Her look in the video — cropped orange hair, man's suit, cane — was a deliberate statement that made her an instant MTV icon.
Yes, those are cows. The video cuts between a boardroom performance and a field of cattle, because Eurythmics wanted it strange.
The song gave the duo their only US number 1 on the Billboard Hot 100, after peaking at number 2 in the UK.
It was the title track of their second album, the record that rescued them from being dropped by their label.
The track has been covered and sampled endlessly — Marilyn Manson's slowed-down 1995 version introduced it to a whole new generation.
In 2023 it entered Spotify's Billions Club, forty years after two broke musicians cooked it up in an attic.

title: Tarzan Boy
description: Pure Italo-disco joy: a jungle-chant chorus and a melody you will be humming for the rest of the day.

pops.text: Baltimora was the stage name of Jimmy McShane, a singer from Northern Ireland who found stardom in Italy's disco scene.
The project was masterminded by Italian producer Maurizio Bassi, who wrote and produced the track in Milan.
That wordless jungle chant in the chorus is the whole hook — a Tarzan-style yodel anyone on Earth can sing along to.
The song was a smash across Europe in 1985 and climbed to number 3 in the UK and number 13 on the Billboard Hot 100.
It became a signature of the Italo-disco wave, when Italian studios pumped out English-language dance hits by the dozen.
McShane's energetic TV performances — all leaps and high kicks — helped sell the record far beyond Italy.
The song got a second life in 1993, turning up in Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles III and a famous mouthwash commercial.
That revival pushed it back onto the Billboard Hot 100 nearly a decade after its first run.
McShane died in 1995, but his one giant hit still fills retro dancefloors from Milan to Milwaukee.

title: This Is Us
description: Two master storytellers flip through a shared photo album, trading verses like an old married couple of song.

pops.text: This duet comes from All the Roadrunning, the collaborative album Knopfler and Harris released in 2006.
Remarkably, that album was recorded in pieces over about seven years, whenever their solo schedules allowed a session.
Knopfler wrote the song as a couple looking back over a life in snapshots — each verse another page of the album.
Harris is country music's most sought-after harmony singer, and her voice wraps around Knopfler's baritone like it was designed to.
This performance is drawn from Real Live Roadrunning, the concert film of their 2006 tour together.
The tour's live album and DVD captured a band of Nashville and London A-listers playing it all without a net.
Knopfler, Dire Straits' frontman, had long wanted to make a full duet record, and Harris was his first and only choice.
The two voices never compete — he tells the story, she answers it, which is exactly the marriage the lyric describes.
Critics greeted the album as a masterclass in restraint — two veterans with nothing left to prove, just listening to each other.

title: Walking in Memphis
description: A piano, a pilgrimage to Memphis, and one of the great songwriter debuts — Graceland, gospel and Beale Street in four minutes.

pops.text: Cohn wrote this after a 1985 trip to Memphis, a pilgrimage he took hoping to shake loose his writer's block. It worked.
The itinerary is the song: Graceland, Beale Street, and the Reverend Al Green's Full Gospel Tabernacle Church, where Cohn heard Green preach.
Muriel is real — Muriel Davis Wilkins played piano every Friday at the Hollywood Cafe in Mississippi, and Cohn sang along with her that night.
She told him to sing like nobody was listening, advice he later said unlocked the whole song.
"Put on my blue suede shoes" nods to Carl Perkins, who recorded his rockabilly classic in Memphis for Sun Studio.
The song was the centerpiece of Cohn's 1991 debut album and reached number 13 on the Billboard Hot 100.
It earned him the Grammy for Best New Artist in 1992, beating out a field that included Boyz II Men.
Cher's 1995 cover became a hit in its own right, reaching number 11 in the UK and introducing the song to a new audience.
Cohn has called it the song that gave him a career; three decades on, it still closes every show he plays.

title: What You Need
description: INXS break America: a swaggering funk-rock strut from Listen Like Thieves with Hutchence in full command.

pops.text: This was the single that finally cracked America for INXS, reaching number 5 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1986.
It comes from Listen Like Thieves, the 1985 album where the Australian band sharpened their funk-rock sound for the world stage.
Producer Chris Thomas, who had worked with the Sex Pistols and Roxy Music, pushed them toward a harder, leaner groove.
Keyboardist and guitarist Andrew Farriss wrote the music; Michael Hutchence supplied the lyric and that strutting vocal.
Kirk Pengilly's sax stabs spar with the Farriss brothers' rhythm groove — a sound the band had honed on Australian stages for years.
Its success dragged the album into the US top 20 and set the table for the stadium-sized Kick two years later.
The video is peak mid-80s INXS — Hutchence working the camera like a man who already knows what's coming.
Australian audiences had known for years; What You Need was the moment US radio programmers caught up.
It remains a fixture of their live legacy, usually placed early to get a crowd moving.

title: Who Can It Be Now?
description: Colin Hay hides from a knock at the door while Greg Ham's saxophone turns paranoia into pure pop.

pops.text: Colin Hay wrote this in 1979, living in a St Kilda apartment block where strangers kept knocking on the wrong door at all hours.
That anxious knock became the song's heartbeat — a hit about wanting the world to just leave you alone.
Greg Ham's saxophone riff is the signature: bright, nagging and impossible to get out of your head.
It was Men At Work's debut single in Australia in 1981, on their first album Business as Usual.
In the US it climbed all the way to number 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 in October 1982.
Business as Usual spent 15 weeks at number 1 in America, an astonishing run for a debut album from Down Under.
The low-budget video, with Hay peering through a door's spyhole, became an early MTV staple.
The band followed it with Down Under, and briefly became the biggest Australian act on the planet.
Hay still performs it acoustically on tour — the paranoia intact, the door knock now supplied by the audience.

title: Wild Wild Life
description: David Byrne throws a lip-sync party and invites everyone — the cheeriest single from the True Stories project.

pops.text: This comes from True Stories, the 1986 Talking Heads album that doubled as the soundtrack to David Byrne's film of the same name.
The video is a karaoke free-for-all: a parade of characters lip-sync the song in a club, each more committed than the last.
Watch for John Goodman, who starred in the film as Louis Fyne, mugging his way through a verse.
Sam Moore of Sam & Dave and guitarist Tito Larriva are among the other familiar faces taking a turn at the mic.
The single reached the US top 30, one of the band's most straightforward pop moments — on purpose.
Byrne wrote the True Stories songs for fictional small-town Texans to sing, then the Heads recorded them as an album too.
The film's cast lip-synced to the band's versions in several scenes, blurring who the song really belonged to.
It won the band a new audience on MTV, where the clip's fancy-dress energy fit the channel perfectly.
The song later lent its name to a Talking Heads concert film reissue and remains their most purely joyful single.

title: Chasing Pirates
description: Norah Jones trades the piano bench for a restless, after-midnight groove on the lead single from The Fall.

pops.text: This was the lead single from The Fall, Jones's fourth studio album, released in 2009.
The Fall was a reinvention: Jones set aside her signature piano-led jazz-pop for guitars, beats and a moodier band sound.
Producer Jacquire King, fresh from Kings of Leon's Only by the Night, ran the sessions in Los Angeles and New York.
Jones wrote the song alone, and its sleepless, prowling lyric matches the album's restless nighttime feel.
She played far more electric guitar on this record, crediting a new band and a deliberate urge to break her own formula.
The single became a mainstay of adult-alternative radio and introduced the album months of touring would be built on.
The Fall debuted at number 3 on the Billboard 200, proof her audience was happy to follow her somewhere new.
A remix EP followed, with versions by Santigold and others pushing the song onto dancefloors — new territory for Jones.
She has said making this record felt like starting over; Chasing Pirates is where you hear that decision most clearly.

title: Young Blood
description: A slow-burning highlight from The Fall — Jones broods over a relationship running on fumes.

pops.text: Young Blood is a deep cut from The Fall, Norah Jones's guitar-driven fourth album from 2009.
Jones co-wrote it with Mike Martin, a member of her touring band, during the album's writing sessions.
Producer Jacquire King gave the track its smoky, echoing atmosphere, a long way from the polish of Come Away with Me.
The lyric looks at a young relationship gone stale — two people going through motions neither believes in anymore.
The Fall sessions split time between studios in Los Angeles and New York, with Jones playing more guitar than ever before.
Critics often single this track out as one of the album's moodiest and most adult moments.
The album's cover photo, shot by Autumn de Wilde, signaled the change: Jones front and center, no piano in sight.
The Fall reached number 3 on the Billboard 200 and topped charts in several countries despite the stylistic swerve.
Young Blood was never a big single, which is exactly why fans treasure it — a quiet stunner hiding mid-album.

title: Ain't That a Kick in the Head
description: Dean Martin, loose and grinning, turns being lovesick into the coolest complaint ever recorded.

pops.text: Songwriting royalty wrote this one: Sammy Cahn and Jimmy Van Heusen, the team behind a string of Sinatra standards.
Martin recorded it in 1960, and it featured in that year's Ocean's 11 — the original Rat Pack heist film, with Dean in the gang.
Nelson Riddle, the arranger behind Sinatra's greatest albums, leads the orchestra on this recording.
The premise is pure Dino: love hits him like a mule kick, and he couldn't sound more delighted about it.
Surprisingly, the single was not a major chart hit on release — its fame grew slowly through film and TV placements.
It has since become one of Martin's signature songs, inseparable from his tuxedo-and-cocktail image.
Video games introduced it to new generations: it beams out of the radios in the Fallout series' retro-future wasteland.
Robbie Williams covered it on his Swing When You're Winning album, one of many singers to borrow Dean's swagger here.
Martin's genius was making it sound effortless — every take sounds like he's telling you the story at a bar, drink in hand.

title: Ooh Child
description: Chicago's first family of soul promises that things are gonna get easier — and you believe every word.

pops.text: The Five Stairsteps were literally a family: the Burke siblings from Chicago, managed by their father, a city police detective.
They earned the nickname "the first family of soul" years before the Jackson 5 made family groups famous.
Songwriter Stan Vincent wrote and produced Ooh Child, tailoring its message of hope for the young group.
Released in 1970 on Buddah Records, it reached number 8 on the Billboard Hot 100 — their biggest hit by far.
The arrangement builds from a gentle opening into that soaring, step-by-step chorus: walk on, walk on.
Curtis Mayfield had signed the group to his label earlier in their career and remained a mentor figure.
The song became an anthem of comfort, covered by everyone from Nina Simone to Hall & Oates.
A new generation met it in Guardians of the Galaxy, where Peter Quill uses it for his famous dance-off distraction — the galaxy, saved by the Stairsteps.
Lead singer Clarence Burke Jr.'s tender delivery still lands like a hand on your shoulder, fifty-plus years later.

title: More Than a Woman
description: Silk falsettos over a disco groove — the Bee Gees at the absolute peak of their Saturday Night Fever powers.

pops.text: The Gibb brothers wrote this for Saturday Night Fever, the 1977 film that turned disco into a worldwide phenomenon.
Two versions appear on the soundtrack: the Bee Gees' own, and a hit single version by Tavares, who took it into the US top 40.
Oddly, the Bee Gees' version was never released as a single in the US at the time — the film and album made it immortal anyway.
The Saturday Night Fever soundtrack became one of the best-selling albums of all time, spending 24 weeks at number 1 in America.
Barry Gibb's falsetto, developed a couple of years earlier, is the sound that defined the Bee Gees' imperial phase.
In the film, the song plays over Tony and Stephanie's rehearsal dance — one of the movie's most romantic sequences.
The brothers wrote much of the Fever material in a rush at a chateau studio in France, working to a film outline.
That French studio, the Chateau d'Herouville, was the same residential setup Elton John had made famous earlier in the decade.
Decades later, the song remains a wedding-and-dancefloor evergreen, its groove instantly recognizable in two bars.

title: Heart and Soul
description: Carol Decker raps, pleads and soars all at once in T'Pau's transatlantic one-hit wonder.

pops.text: First, the name: T'Pau comes from a Vulcan elder in Star Trek — the band were unabashed fans of the original series.
Singer Carol Decker and guitarist Ron Rogers wrote the song, building it around her overlapping, call-and-response vocals.
It was first released in the UK in 1986 and flopped — then a jeans commercial put it on TV and everything changed.
Re-released in 1987, it stormed to number 4 on both the UK chart and the Billboard Hot 100.
The layered vocal was so distinctive that Decker had to work out how to perform it live with backing singers covering the echoes.
It anchored their debut album Bridge of Spies, which went multi-platinum in Britain.
In the US, T'Pau are filed under one-hit wonders — this was their only American top-40 single.
At home it was a different story: China in Your Hand, from the same album, spent five weeks at UK number 1.
The song's breathless energy still makes it a first pick for 80s compilations and karaoke nights alike.

title: Roxanne
description: Sting pleads with a Parisian streetwalker over a tango-reggae groove — the song that launched The Police.

pops.text: Sting wrote this in Paris in 1977, after the struggling band played a near-empty gig and he noticed the women working near their seedy hotel.
Her name came from a poster for Cyrano de Bergerac in the hotel foyer — Roxanne is the play's heroine.
Hear that odd piano chord and laugh at the very start? Sting accidentally sat on a piano keyboard in the studio, and they kept it in.
The band recorded it at Surrey Sound Studios on a shoestring budget, borrowing studio time between other acts' sessions.
First released in April 1978, it went nowhere. Re-released in 1979, it climbed to number 12 in the UK and cracked the US top 40.
Its tango-meets-reggae rhythm was unlike anything else on the radio, announcing the Police sound in one song.
Sting has said the lyric was written as a genuine love song, not a joke — he wanted Roxanne treated as a person, not a punchline.
The song became so big that Sting later reworked it as a jazzy showpiece, and it anchored the band's 2007 reunion tour setlists.
It was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame, a long way from that empty Paris club.

title: Every Little Thing She Does Is Magic
description: Sting's oldest love song finally gets its moment — piano-driven, joyful, and one of The Police's biggest singles.

pops.text: Believe it or not, Sting wrote this in 1976, before The Police had even formed — then waited five years to record it properly.
An early demo sat in a drawer because the song's bright pop feel didn't fit the band's early punk-reggae image.
It finally landed on Ghost in the Machine in 1981, recorded at AIR Studios on the Caribbean island of Montserrat.
The piano that drives the song was played by session musician Jean Roussel, giving it a bounce unlike any other Police track.
The video was filmed at the Montserrat studio itself — the band clowning around the control room and pool between takes.
It became a transatlantic smash: number 3 in both the UK and on the Billboard Hot 100.
Sting has called it a song about unrequited longing dressed up as celebration — the singer never actually gets the girl.
Ghost in the Machine, named after an Arthur Koestler book, topped the UK album chart and hit number 2 in the US.
The song's afterlife includes countless wedding playlists — that chorus was simply built to be sung back.

title: Don't Dream It's Over
description: Neil Finn's hymn to holding on — a debut-album single that became one of the most beloved songs of the 80s.

pops.text: Neil Finn wrote this at his family's home in New Zealand, sitting at the piano feeling like the world was against him — then choosing defiance.
It was the fourth single from Crowded House's 1986 debut album, after Finn's previous band Split Enz had called it a day.
The song climbed to number 2 on the Billboard Hot 100 and became the band's American signature.
Producer Mitchell Froom's organ swells give the chorus its cathedral lift; Froom would shape the band's sound for years.
The surreal video, full of floating household objects and a house filling with clutter, won fans on MTV worldwide.
In Australia and New Zealand it was a number 1-level anthem, and it has never really left the radio there since.
Finn has performed it at moments of national mourning and celebration alike — it has become part of New Zealand's emotional furniture.
Miley Cyrus and Ariana Grande's acoustic cover in 2015 introduced it to a new generation and raised money for charity.
Finn later joined Fleetwood Mac on stage, where this song — by then a standard — fit right into their set.

title: Never Surrender
description: Canada's sunglassed pop star delivers a fist-in-the-air anthem about refusing to give up on your dreams.

pops.text: Montreal's Corey Hart wrote this as a pep talk to himself, after years of record-label rejections before his breakthrough.
It was the lead single from Boy in the Box, his 1985 second album, and it raced to number 3 on the Billboard Hot 100.
In Canada it was even bigger, winning the Juno Award for Single of the Year.
Boy in the Box went diamond in Canada — a million copies — making Hart one of the country's biggest-ever pop exports.
The song's theme was Hart's life story: he had been turned down by labels in two countries before Sunglasses at Night hit.
Speaking of which — yes, he really did become famous wearing sunglasses, a look inspired by a photoshoot on a blindingly bright day.
Never Surrender became a graduation and sports-arena staple, its chorus purpose-built for chanting along.
Hart stepped away from pop stardom in the 90s to raise his family, later returning on his own terms.
In 2019 he was inducted into the Canadian Music Hall of Fame, performing this song at the Juno Awards to a standing ovation.

title: Be Near Me
description: Martin Fry in a gold suit, begging beautifully — ABC's sleekest single and their biggest American hit.

pops.text: ABC, the Sheffield band who helped invent 80s sophisti-pop, released this in 1985 on their third album, How to Be a... Zillionaire!
It became their biggest hit in America, reaching number 9 on the Billboard Hot 100.
Frontman Martin Fry, he of the famous gold lame suit, co-wrote and co-produced the band's material with Mark White.
By this album the group had slimmed to a duo — Fry and White — leaning hard into synths, drum machines and cartoon-bright pop.
The Zillionaire album even came with animated alter egos for the pair, years before Gorillaz made that a business model.
Be Near Me's pleading lyric over a clinical electronic groove is peak ABC: heartbreak dressed for a champagne reception.
The band's earlier album The Lexicon of Love is now routinely ranked among the greatest debuts ever made.
Fry kept ABC touring for decades, and the orchestral Lexicon of Love shows became a beloved fixture in the UK.
In the US, though, this is the one — the song American radio never let go of.

title: Son of a Preacher Man
description: Dusty goes to Memphis and comes back with soul music's most smoldering sermon — a top-10 triumph on both sides of the Atlantic.

pops.text: Writers John Hurley and Ronnie Wilkins composed this with Aretha Franklin in mind — her father was a famous preacher, after all.
Aretha passed on it. Dusty Springfield recorded it in Memphis instead, and it became the signature hit of her career.
The sessions were at American Sound Studio for the album Dusty in Memphis, produced by Jerry Wexler, Tom Dowd and Arif Mardin.
Dusty was so intimidated singing alongside Memphis's finest musicians that she initially struggled to finish her vocals.
Released in late 1968, it hit number 9 in the UK and number 10 in the US — her last big American hit.
Aretha eventually recorded her own version in 1969, after Dusty's success proved the song's power.
Dusty in Memphis flopped commercially at first, then grew into one of the most acclaimed albums ever made — it sits in the Grammy Hall of Fame and the US National Recording Registry.
Quentin Tarantino revived the song for Pulp Fiction in 1994, sending a new generation hunting for Dusty's records.
Her smoky, knowing delivery here is the blueprint every blue-eyed soul singer since has studied.

title: Throwing It All Away
description: Genesis say goodbye with a shrug and a perfect pop chorus — the bittersweet heart of Invisible Touch.

pops.text: This was a single from Invisible Touch, the 1986 album that turned Genesis into the biggest band in the world.
Mike Rutherford wrote the lyric — a shrug of a breakup song, listing everything being walked away from.
The music grew out of a Rutherford guitar riff the band jammed on at their studio, The Farm, in Surrey, England.
It reached number 4 on the Billboard Hot 100, one of five top-5 singles from the album in America.
The video is a patchwork of the band's own home movies — backstage goofing, soundchecks and life on the road.
That loose, candid footage was a deliberate contrast to the slick, high-concept clips dominating MTV in 1986.
Invisible Touch sold millions and made Phil Collins, Tony Banks and Rutherford unlikely pop superstars in their late thirties.
The song's gentle jangle hides a cold little lyric: not a plea to stay, just an inventory of what's being thrown away.
It remains a staple of Collins-era Genesis nostalgia tours — the crowd always sings the title line back.

title: This Must Be the Place (Naive Melody)
description: David Byrne writes a straight-up love song — warm, wobbly and quietly one of the greatest things Talking Heads ever did.

pops.text: David Byrne has called this a love song written without irony — a genuine first for rock's most famously anxious frontman.
It's from Speaking in Tongues, the 1983 album that also gave the band their only US top-10 single, Burning Down the House.
The subtitle is the method: "naive melody" because the band members played parts on instruments that weren't their main ones, keeping everything simple.
Tina Weymouth and Jerry Harrison traded their usual roles around the song's gentle, circling keyboard figure.
Session ace Wally Badarou added the shimmering synth textures that make the track glow.
As a single it only grazed the charts, but over the years it grew into arguably the band's most beloved song.
In the concert film Stop Making Sense, Byrne performs it while slow-dancing with a floor lamp — one of cinema's great music moments.
The lyric's home-is-where-you-are sentiment has made it a wedding-song staple, covered by everyone from Arcade Fire to Kermit the Frog.
Byrne still closes chapters of his career with it — it was the emotional peak of his American Utopia stage show and film.

title: Danke Schoen
description: A 21-year-old Wayne Newton says thank you very much — and a German thank-you becomes an all-American standard.

pops.text: "Danke schoen" is simply German for "thank you very much" — and in 1963, America couldn't stop saying it.
The song's music was written by German bandleader Bert Kaempfert, with English lyrics by Milt Gabler.
It was first meant for Bobby Darin, who heard young Wayne Newton sing and insisted the kid record it instead.
Newton was just 21, and Darin backed him — producing and championing the record that became Newton's breakthrough.
The single reached number 13 on the Billboard Hot 100 and turned Newton into a national teen-era star.
He parlayed it into one of the great Las Vegas careers, eventually earning the nickname Mr. Las Vegas.
A whole new generation learned the song from Ferris Bueller's Day Off, where Ferris lip-syncs it on a parade float in Chicago.
That 1986 film moment sent the record back into the culture for good — it's now inseparable from Ferris's perfect day off.
Newton performed the song for over half a century; the thank-you, clearly, was mutual.

title: Jet Airliner
description: Steve Miller turns someone else's shelved song into a first-class classic-rock boarding call.

pops.text: Pop-up fact: Steve Miller did not write this one. Singer-songwriter Paul Pena penned it in 1973.
That synth swoosh up front is called Threshold — on the album it melts straight into this song.
Pena's own album sat unreleased for decades because of label trouble, so almost nobody heard his version first.
Miller heard Pena's record through Ben Sidran, a keyboard player who had worked with both men.
The band cut the track during the same fertile run that produced Fly Like an Eagle.
It rides on Book of Dreams, the 1977 album Miller recorded as a companion to that Eagle success.
As a single it climbed to No. 8 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1977.
Miller trimmed and brightened Pena's folkier original, pushing that chugging guitar riff to the front.
Decades of classic-rock radio later, that big ol' jet airliner still has not carried the song away.

title: Hello New Orleans
description: A Texas storyteller tips his hat to the Crescent City, horns, hunger and all.

pops.text: Pop-up fact: Texas songwriter Robert Earl Keen opens his album Gravitational Forces with a love letter to another state entirely.
Gravitational Forces arrived in 2001 on the Lost Highway label, a fitting home for Keen's literary country songs.
Keen built his following the slow way — house concerts, college towns and songs other songwriters wished they had written.
He famously shared a house in College Station with a young Lyle Lovett back in their Texas A&M days.
The track rolls on a loose, front-porch groove that nods to the New Orleans parade beat in its bones.
Keen's writing trademark is all here: specific places, working people and choruses built for a room to sing back.
The album paired him with producer Gurf Morlix, a key figure in the Austin roots-music scene.
Keen announced his retirement from touring in 2022, then — happily for fans — kept finding reasons to play select shows.
For a songwriter from Houston, Keen sure sounds at home the second this one lands in New Orleans.

title: Something Less Than Something More
description: Two North Carolina voices lean into each other on a duet about almost-love.

pops.text: Pop-up fact: This is a true co-write — Caitlin Cary and Thad Cockrell share both the songwriting and the singing.
Cary first turned heads as the fiddle player and harmony singer in Whiskeytown, alongside Ryan Adams.
The song comes from Begonias, the pair's 2005 duets album on North Carolina's Yep Roc Records.
Cockrell brought a high, lonesome tenor shaped by gospel and classic country; Cary brought the ache.
The two met through the fertile Raleigh-Chapel Hill alt-country scene of the late 1990s.
Begonias was produced with a light touch, leaving the two voices and the space between them to do the work.
Critics praised the record as a modern take on the great country duet tradition of George and Tammy.
The title phrase is the whole heartbreak in one line — close to love, never quite arriving.
No video was ever made for this deep cut, which is exactly why album tracks like it are worth digging up.

title: Still Pretending
description: A Raleigh songwriter confesses that the welcome mat is out but the heart is not fooled.

pops.text: Pop-up fact: Tift Merritt wrote this one alone, and it remains one of her signature songs.
It comes from Tambourine, her 2004 album that earned a Grammy nomination for Best Country Album — despite sounding more like Memphis soul.
Tambourine was produced by George Drakoulias and featured Heartbreaker Mike Campbell on guitar.
Merritt grew up in Raleigh, North Carolina, and started out playing the Triangle's clubs and coffeehouses.
The lyric's small domestic details — a driveway, a ribbon in her hair — do the emotional heavy lifting.
Before Tambourine, her debut Bramble Rose had critics comparing her to Emmylou Harris.
She recorded much of Tambourine chasing a Dusty in Memphis warmth, all horns and late-night glow.
Merritt later revisited the song in stripped-down kitchen recordings, proof of how sturdy the writing is.
This live clip catches the song the way her fans love it most — close, quiet and completely unpretending.

title: The Rubberband Man
description: Philly soul at its stretchiest — a street performer's act turned into a No. 1 soul smash.

pops.text: Pop-up fact: Producer Thom Bell wrote this with Linda Creed, inspired by Bell's own son and his rubber-band tricks.
It was the Spinners' last big hit with lead singer Philippe Wynne's joyful ad-libs all over it.
The record comes from Happiness Is Being with the Spinners, released in 1976.
Bell recorded it in Philadelphia with MFSB, the house band behind the whole Philly soul sound.
The single shot to No. 1 on Billboard's soul chart and No. 2 on the Hot 100.
On TV the group performed it with giant rubber bands worked into the choreography — hard to forget once seen.
Wynne's scatting outro is pure improvisation, the sound of a singer having the time of his life.
The song found a whole new audience in 2018 when it sound-tracked the Guardians of the Galaxy's entrance in Avengers: Infinity War.
Nearly fifty years on, that bassline still snaps back like, well, you know.

title: Hang On Sloopy
description: Three chords, one teenage lead singer, and a garage-rock chant that became a state song.

pops.text: Pop-up fact: Lead singer Rick Zehringer was just 17 — he soon renamed himself Rick Derringer and became a guitar hero.
The song began life as My Girl Sloopy, a 1964 R&B single by the Vibrations.
Writers Bert Berns and Wes Farrell reworked it, and Berns released the McCoys' version on his brand-new Bang Records.
The hit actually uses a backing track first cut for the Strangeloves, with young Rick's vocal laid on top.
It hit No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 in October 1965, briefly wedged between Barry McGuire and the Beatles.
The McCoys hailed from Union City, Indiana — about as garage-band America as it gets.
Ohio State's marching band adopted it in 1965, starting one of college football's great singalong traditions.
In 1985 Ohio made it the state's official rock song — the first state ever to claim one.
Derringer later topped the charts again with Rock and Roll, Hoochie Koo and produced Weird Al. Sloopy started it all.

title: (Sittin' On) the Dock of the Bay
description: The saddest whistle in soul music, recorded days before the plane crash that took its singer.

pops.text: Pop-up fact: Otis Redding started writing this on a houseboat in Sausalito after playing the Monterey Pop Festival.
He finished it with guitarist Steve Cropper at Stax Records in Memphis in late 1967.
That gentle guitar figure is Cropper, who also co-wrote Midnight Hour and Green Onions.
Redding recorded the final vocal just days before his death in a plane crash on December 10, 1967.
The whistled ending was a placeholder — Otis meant to come back and write a final verse.
Released in January 1968, it became the first posthumous No. 1 single in US chart history.
It topped both the pop and R&B charts and won two Grammy Awards.
The seagull and wave sounds were added in the studio to put you right there on that dock.
Rolling Stone ranks it among the greatest songs ever made — and that unfinished whistle still says everything.

title: Rock Your Baby
description: The demo that accidentally launched disco, sung by a guy who just happened to be in the studio.

pops.text: Pop-up fact: This was written and produced by Harry Wayne Casey and Richard Finch — KC and his Sunshine Band partner.
The backing track was cut in about 45 minutes as a demo, built around guitarist Jerome Smith's hypnotic riff.
Casey could not hit the high notes himself, so the song waited for the right singer.
George McCrae happened to be at TK Studios in Hialeah, Florida — his wife Gwen had been asked to sing it, and George stepped in instead.
McCrae nailed that falsetto in a couple of takes, and a landmark was born.
It hit No. 1 on the Hot 100 in July 1974 and topped the UK chart for three weeks.
Often called one of the first disco hits, it sold in the millions worldwide before disco even had a name.
John Lennon later said it helped inspire his own No. 1, Whatever Gets You Thru the Night.
ABBA's Bjorn and Benny were fans too — listen for its DNA in Dancing Queen's glide.

title: Our House
description: Seven nutty Londoners cram a whole childhood into one terraced house in the middle of the street.

pops.text: Pop-up fact: Guitarist Chris Foreman and sax man Cathal Smyth wrote it about growing up in crowded working-class homes.
It was released in November 1982 from the album The Rise & Fall.
The video's chaotic family home was a real terraced house at 47 Stephenson Street in northwest London.
Watch for the cutaways to Buckingham Palace and the Playboy Mansion — same lyric, slightly bigger houses.
The clip's slapstick door routine was borrowed from the Keystone Kops and Benny Hill, the band cheerfully admitted.
Heavy MTV rotation made this Madness's only US Top 10 hit, peaking at No. 7.
Back home it reached No. 5 and won the Ivor Novello Award for Best Pop Song.
The song later gave its name to the hit Madness jukebox musical Our House in London's West End.
It even opened the 2012 London Olympics closing ceremony — the whole country knew every word.

title: Come Fly With Me
description: Sinatra and Billy May pack a suitcase full of swing for the jet age's favorite invitation.

pops.text: Pop-up fact: Jimmy Van Heusen and Sammy Cahn wrote this expressly for Sinatra — it is the title track of his 1958 travel-themed album.
The album was arranged by Billy May, whose brassy, swooping charts became a Sinatra signature.
That famous cover shows Frank in front of a TWA jet — pure early jet-age glamour.
The lyric's itinerary name-checks Bombay, Peru and Acapulco Bay, exotic stuff in 1958.
Cahn and Van Heusen were Sinatra's house songwriters — they also gave him High Hopes and All the Way.
This live version comes from his 1965 TV special A Man and His Music, Frank at his tuxedoed peak.
The album was one of the first Sinatra concepts built around a single theme: getting out of town in style.
It reached the top of the album charts and stayed a Sinatra calling card for the rest of his career.
Airlines have borrowed the title ever since. None of them swing like this.

title: The Way You Look Tonight
description: An Oscar-winning standard from a Fred Astaire movie, made immortal a second time by Sinatra.

pops.text: Pop-up fact: Jerome Kern and Dorothy Fields wrote this for the 1936 film Swing Time, where Fred Astaire sang it to Ginger Rogers.
It won the Academy Award for Best Original Song — Fields was the first woman to win that Oscar.
Sinatra recorded his definitive version in 1964 for an album devoted entirely to Academy Award winners.
The arrangement is by Nelson Riddle, Sinatra's greatest collaborator, all warmth and strings.
Frank had actually sung it on radio back in the 1940s — he lived with the song for decades.
Astaire's original single was a hit in 1936; Sinatra's reading made it a standard for the ages.
The lyric's trick is its tenderness: it is a love song addressed to a memory of tonight.
Michael Buble, Tony Bennett and Rod Stewart all cut it later — everyone measures themselves against Frank here.
Some day, when you're awfully low, this is the version that will feel like a glow.

title: I Get a Kick Out of You
description: Cole Porter's champagne-flat confession, delivered by the one singer who made everything sound like a kick.

pops.text: Pop-up fact: Cole Porter wrote this for his 1934 Broadway hit Anything Goes, where Ethel Merman introduced it.
The original lyric name-checked a famous aviator's wife; Porter swapped lines over the years as headlines changed.
Sinatra first recorded it for Capitol in the 1950s and kept it in his act for forty years.
This performance comes from his 1957 television show — Frank loose, grinning and swinging hard.
He also cut a celebrated version on the 1962 album Sinatra and Swingin' Brass with arranger Neal Hefti.
Porter's champagne line was cheeky in 1934: a love song that opens by shrugging at luxury itself.
Gary Barlow, Jamie Cullum and Lady Gaga with Tony Bennett have all revived it since.
Sinatra loved Porter — he starred in the Porter biopic-era film Can-Can and recorded a full Porter songbook's worth of tunes.
That little extra boot he throws into the last line? Pure Sinatra, never on the page.

title: Black Crow
description: Diana Krall takes a Joni Mitchell restlessness anthem and flies it low over late-night piano.

pops.text: Pop-up fact: Joni Mitchell wrote Black Crow for her 1976 album Hejira, her great record about life on the road.
Krall's version anchors The Girl in the Other Room, her 2004 album and a turning point in her career.
That album was the first where Krall co-wrote originals, several with her new husband, Elvis Costello.
It was produced by Tommy LiPuma and recorded with guitarist Anthony Wilson's supple trio backing.
The Girl in the Other Room topped jazz charts and reached the US Top 5 — huge for a jazz record.
This performance was filmed at the Montreal Jazz Festival in June 2004, Krall on home Canadian turf.
Mitchell is a fellow Canadian and a Krall hero; Krall later returned the favor across her whole catalog of standards.
The crow in the lyric dives for anything shiny — Mitchell's perfect image of the touring life.
Krall slows the flight down until every feather shows. Same sky, different weather.

title: Just the Way You Are
description: Billy Joel's promise of unconditional love, re-dressed in Parisian torch-song silk.

pops.text: Pop-up fact: Billy Joel wrote this for his first wife — it won the Grammy for Song of the Year in 1979.
Joel nearly left it off The Stranger; producer Phil Ramone and his band talked him into keeping it.
Krall's version was filmed for Live in Paris, recorded at the Olympia in 2001 and released in 2002.
The Paris band is a dream team: Anthony Wilson on guitar, John Clayton on bass, Jeff Hamilton on drums.
Claus Ogerman's orchestral arrangements wrap the trio in the same luxury he gave The Look of Love album.
Live in Paris became Krall's first No. 1 jazz album and a Grammy winner for Best Jazz Vocal Album.
Joel himself was famously ambivalent about the song for years — wedding gigs will do that — but covers like this restore its glow.
Barry White also cut a hit version in 1978; Krall's is the one that whispers instead of testifies.
Don't go changing — Krall does not. She just changes the lighting.

title: 'S Wonderful
description: The Gershwins' 1927 compliment, burnished by Krall and Claus Ogerman's orchestra into pure glamour.

pops.text: Pop-up fact: George and Ira Gershwin wrote this in 1927 for the stage musical Funny Face, starring Fred and Adele Astaire.
The title's dropped letter was pure Ira wordplay — wonderful was not quite wonderful enough.
Krall's version opens her 2001 album The Look of Love, arranged and conducted by Claus Ogerman.
Ogerman had arranged the classic bossa nova records of the 1960s; you can hear that elegance all over this.
The Look of Love became Krall's breakthrough, topping the Canadian charts and going multi-platinum.
The album was produced by Tommy LiPuma and engineered by the legendary Al Schmitt.
Funny Face later became a film with Audrey Hepburn, who sang this very song on screen.
Krall recorded it at Capitol Studios in Hollywood — the Gershwins meet the Sinatra room.
'S marvelous how a song from 1927 still lands like a first compliment.

title: Look at Miss Ohio
description: Two guitars, two voices, and a beauty queen who wants to do right — but not right now.

pops.text: Pop-up fact: Gillian Welch wrote this with her musical partner David Rawlings, as she writes everything — the two are inseparable co-writers.
It opens Soul Journey, Welch's 2003 album, her loosest and most electric-leaning record.
Welch and Rawlings famously sound like a lost 1930s duo despite both being modern, conservatory-sharp players.
Rawlings plays a small 1935 Epiphone archtop guitar — that wiry, inverted harmony guitar sound is all his own invention.
The pair met at Berklee College of Music in Boston, bonding over old-time and bluegrass records.
Welch's big break came when Emmylou Harris recorded her Orphan Girl, before Welch had an album out.
The Miss Ohio lyric is pure Welch: a pageant smile over a runaway heart, judged by nobody.
Miranda Lambert cut a celebrated cover, carrying the song to a whole new audience.
This vinyl video is just the record turning — fitting for music that has always sounded timeless.

title: What Is Life
description: The quiet Beatle bursts out of the band's shadow with a wall-of-sound love song to everything.

pops.text: Pop-up fact: Harrison wrote this in 1969, originally thinking of offering it to Billy Preston.
It erupts from All Things Must Pass, the 1970 triple album that announced Harrison as a solo giant.
Phil Spector co-produced, piling on the famous Wall of Sound — that glow is dozens of musicians deep.
The backing band includes Eric Clapton and the members of Badfinger on acoustic guitars and tambourine.
Released as a single in 1971, it hit the Top 10 in the US alongside My Sweet Lord's reign.
All Things Must Pass was the first triple album by a solo artist and the best-selling solo Beatle debut.
This official video arrived decades later, in 2014, from a fan contest run by Olivia and Dhani Harrison — a ballet in a pine forest won.
Harrison had stockpiled songs for years while Lennon and McCartney filled the Beatles' albums. This is the floodgate opening.
What is life without your love? Fifty years later the question still sounds like joy, not doubt.

title: Rich Girl
description: Hall & Oates' first No. 1 — and plot twist: the rich girl was actually a rich guy.

pops.text: Pop-up fact: Daryl Hall wrote this about a real person — a spoiled ex-boyfriend of his girlfriend Sara Allen. Yes, a guy.
Hall changed the gender because a rich guy lyric did not sing as well. The secret stayed hidden for years.
It was the duo's first No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100, topping the chart in March 1977.
The song came from the 1976 album Bigger Than Both of Us, cut in Los Angeles.
Hall and Oates met in Philadelphia in 1967 — famously ducking into the same elevator to escape a gang fight at a dance.
Sara Allen inspired several songs, including their earlier hit Sara Smile.
The track's blue-eyed soul groove was built with top LA session players, a new polish for the duo.
Its chorus raised a few eyebrows on 1970s radio — Hall has always shrugged and pointed to the songwriting.
Nina Simone and later country star Sara Evans both covered it. Rich Girl keeps changing fortunes.

title: I'm a Believer
description: A TV band, a Neil Diamond song, and the best-selling single of 1967 — believe it.

pops.text: Pop-up fact: A young Neil Diamond wrote this — he recorded his own version a year after the Monkees made it immortal.
Micky Dolenz sings lead, though Davy Jones fronted many of the group's other hits.
It was released in November 1966 and spent seven weeks at No. 1 in the US.
It became the biggest-selling single of 1967, powered by the Monkees' hit NBC television show.
Session pros, including Diamond's own guitarist, played the track — the Monkees were still fighting to play on their records.
The B-side, Steppin' Stone, became a punk-era standard in its own right. Some flip side.
Diamond reportedly wanted to keep the song for himself; producer Jeff Barry knew a smash when he heard one.
Smash Mouth's cover for Shrek in 2001 sent it to No. 1 with a whole new generation of kids.
Then I saw her face — and pop history changed. This live clip shows the mania was real.

title: Come Go With Me
description: Air Force buddies in Pittsburgh harmonize their way into doo-wop history — dum dum dum, indeed.

pops.text: Pop-up fact: The Del-Vikings formed in 1955 among US Air Force servicemen stationed in Pittsburgh.
Bass singer Clarence Quick wrote this in the barracks — he sings that famous low dum-dum-dum intro figure.
Lead vocal is by Norman Wright, just a teenager when the group formed.
First released on tiny Fee Bee Records in 1956, it exploded when Dot Records picked it up nationally in 1957.
It peaked at No. 4 on the pop chart and No. 2 on the R&B chart, selling over a million copies.
The group was unusually integrated for the 1950s — Black and white airmen singing together on stage and on TV.
Legal tangles briefly split them into two competing Del-Vikings lineups recording at once.
The song later turned up in American Graffiti, Diner and Stand by Me — Hollywood's favorite 50s cue.
The Beach Boys and Dion both covered it, but nobody dum-dums like the originals.

title: Treme Song
description: New Orleans' own voice sings his neighborhood back to life — and becomes the sound of a TV era.

pops.text: Pop-up fact: John Boutte grew up in the Treme itself, one of America's oldest Black neighborhoods and a cradle of jazz.
He wrote this celebration of the neighborhood long before television came calling.
In 2010 it became the main-title theme of HBO's Treme, David Simon's post-Katrina New Orleans drama.
Boutte comes from a musical family — his sister Lillian Boutte is a noted jazz singer who took him on tour in Europe.
Before music took over, Boutte served in the US Army and worked his way up in a credit union.
The song name-checks the second lines, parades and porch life that define the neighborhood's rhythm.
The Treme soundtrack album featuring this track was nominated for a Grammy.
Boutte still lives and sings in New Orleans — locals simply call him the voice of the city.
These are the actual HBO opening titles: brass, beads and a neighborhood that would not drown.

title: This City
description: Steve Earle writes New Orleans a survival vow in one morning, then watches his TV character sing it into legend.

pops.text: Pop-up fact: Earle wrote this in a single morning after Treme creator David Simon asked for a song his character would have written in 2005.
Earle played street musician Harley Watt on the show — this song closes the first season finale.
It was produced by T Bone Burnett with arrangements by New Orleans legend Allen Toussaint.
The recording happened fast at Piety Street Studios in New Orleans' Bywater neighborhood.
Earle later included it on his 2011 album I'll Never Get Out of This World Alive.
The song earned both Grammy and Emmy nominations — rare air for a TV-born tune.
In the show, the lyric is workshopped on screen with violinist Annie, played by Lucia Micarelli.
Earle knew the territory: he had acted for Simon before, playing a recovering addict sponsor on The Wire.
This city won't ever die — after Katrina, that was not a lyric. It was a promise.

title: Feels Like Rain
description: A slow Louisiana storm of a love song from the album that finally made John Hiatt undeniable.

pops.text: Pop-up fact: This comes from Slow Turning, Hiatt's 1988 album, widely considered his masterpiece run alongside Bring the Family.
The band behind him includes slide guitarist Sonny Landreth, whose swampy touch is all over the record.
Hiatt wrote it soaked in Louisiana imagery — the river meeting the sea down below New Orleans.
Bonnie Raitt was a key Hiatt champion; she cut his Thing Called Love and took it onto her Grammy-winning Nick of Time.
Buddy Guy later made Feels Like Rain the title track of his own Grammy-winning 1993 blues album.
Hiatt had been dropped by labels and battled addiction before this late-80s creative rebirth in his mid-30s.
The song was never a big single for Hiatt himself — it grew the slow way, cover by cover, fan by fan.
Aaron Neville and countless bar bands have kept it in the New Orleans songbook ever since.
Love comes out of nowhere, like a hurricane — and this one has been raining for nearly forty years.

title: Evil Woman
description: Jeff Lynne writes a kiss-off in half an hour and lands ELO's first worldwide hit.
