pops.text: Pop-up fact: Jeff Lynne has said he wrote this in about thirty minutes, near the end of the Face the Music sessions, because the album needed one more track.
Face the Music arrived in 1975, ELO's fifth album, recorded in Munich, Germany.
It became the band's first worldwide hit, reaching the Top 10 in both the US and UK.
That stabbing piano riff and string attack were Lynne's formula perfected: Beatles melody meets orchestra.
Lynne produced it himself, as he did nearly everything — singer, writer, guitarist and studio architect in one.
The song got a second UK chart life in 1978 when it was reissued on an ELO EP.
It later popped up everywhere from Austin Powers in Goldmember to Grand Theft Auto IV.
ELO's spaceship-stage era was still ahead; this is the hit that paid for liftoff.
Thirty minutes to write, fifty years on the radio. Not a bad afternoon's work.

title: Heard It in a Love Song
description: Southern rock's gentlest goodbye, carried on a flute line you can hum from memory.

pops.text: Pop-up fact: Guitarist Toy Caldwell wrote this — and famously picked his lead guitar with his thumb, no pick, ever.
It was the band's highest-charting pop single, reaching No. 14 on the Hot 100 in 1977.
The song comes from Carolina Dreams, the Spartanburg, South Carolina band's 1977 album.
That floating flute is Jerry Eubanks, the Marshall Tucker Band's secret weapon on flute and sax.
Vocalist Doug Gray delivers the lyric sweet as tea — even though the narrator is leaving town for good.
Listen closely: the hit single version trims the album cut's long instrumental ride.
The band took its name from a key tag left in their rehearsal space by a local piano tuner named Marshall Tucker — a real man, not a member.
Carolina Dreams went platinum and put the band on arena bills with the Allman Brothers' generation of Southern rockers.
Country star Mark Chesnutt later titled a whole album after it. Can't say it plainer than that.

title: Dixie Chicken
description: Lowell George's New Orleans-soaked tall tale of a smooth-talking stranger and the woman who out-foxed every man in town — Little Feat's signature song.

pops.text: Title track of Little Feat's third album, released in January 1973 — the record where the band's whole sound clicked into place.
Lowell George wrote it with Fred 'Martin' Kibbee, an old friend from his pre-Feat days in Los Angeles.
George produced the album himself, leaning hard into the New Orleans funk and R&B he adored.
That greasy groove is Bill Payne's piano doing the heavy lifting — Payne co-founded the band with George in 1969.
The lyric is a barroom confession: the narrator blew everything on a woman, then finds a whole bar full of men singing the same story.
New members Kenny Gradney, Sam Clayton and Paul Barrere joined just before this album, giving Feat its classic six-piece lineup.
Album cover artist Neon Park painted the surreal sleeve — he became the band's visual signature through the decade.
A live version opens the band's beloved 1978 live album Waiting for Columbus, recorded in London and Washington, D.C.
Bonnie Raitt and Emmylou Harris sang backup when the band played it on The Midnight Special in 1977 — peak seventies, right there.

title: Willin'
description: The great American trucker ballad — a smuggler's confession sung low and easy, and the song that launched Little Feat out of Frank Zappa's band.

pops.text: Lowell George wrote this while he was still a member of Frank Zappa's Mothers of Invention.
When George played it for Zappa, Zappa reportedly told him he should go form his own band — so he did.
Country singer Johnny Darrell actually recorded the song first, on his 1970 album California Stop-Over.
This debut-album version from 1971 features Ry Cooder guesting on bottleneck guitar.
Unhappy with the tempo, the band re-recorded it slower for their second album, Sailin' Shoes, in 1972 — that take became the famous one.
The re-recording swaps Cooder's bottleneck for Sneaky Pete Kleinow's pedal steel, and the whole song relaxes into its loping groove.
One honest line about 'weed, whites and wine' kept the song off most American radio playlists for years.
Linda Ronstadt covered it on her 1974 breakthrough album Heart Like a Wheel, carrying it to a much bigger audience.
Truckers adopted it as an anthem — Tucson to Tucumcari, Tehachapi to Tonopah is a real southwest trucking route, give or take a detour.

title: Like the Weather
description: Natalie Merchant turns a gray, can't-get-out-of-bed mood into the sunniest-sounding single of 1987 — jangle-pop with a storm cloud inside.

pops.text: From In My Tribe, the 1987 album that took 10,000 Maniacs from college-radio cult act to the mainstream.
Natalie Merchant wrote the song — a peppy melody wrapped around a lyric about being too low to face the day.
Producer Peter Asher, famous for his work with James Taylor and Linda Ronstadt, gave the band its polished folk-pop sheen.
The video was directed by Adrian Edmondson — yes, Vyvyan from The Young Ones — and it helped break the band on MTV.
The single reached No. 68 on the Billboard Hot 100, the band's first real chart foothold.
In My Tribe stayed on the album chart for 77 weeks and went on to sell over two million copies.
The band formed in Jamestown, New York, in 1981, taking their name from a low-budget horror film title.
Merchant was barely into her twenties here, already writing about child abuse, illiteracy and war elsewhere on this album.
Elektra pushed the song with a 20-minute longform promo video pairing the clip with a Merchant interview — very 1988.

title: Don't Talk
description: A fed-up lover's plea set to chiming guitars — Merchant asks for silence and honesty over another round of drunken talk.

pops.text: The opening single salvo from In My Tribe, released in 1987 on Elektra Records.
The lyric addresses an alcoholic partner: all that talk when drinking means nothing by morning.
Natalie Merchant wrote the words; guitarist Robert Buck's chiming, melodic playing carries the track.
The video was directed by Sebastian Harris and later collected on the band's Time Capsule video compilation.
Producer Peter Asher recorded the album in Los Angeles, a long way from the band's Jamestown, New York roots.
Live, this song was a showcase for Buck — fans still talk about the extended guitar solo he stretched out at the end.
In My Tribe tackled heavy subjects across its tracklist, and this was its most direct song about addiction.
The band performed the song on their 1993 MTV Unplugged appearance, near the end of Merchant's tenure.
Merchant left in 1993 for a solo career; the Maniacs carried on, but this album remains their defining statement.

title: The Painted Desert
description: A daydream in song form — two separated lovers keep promising to meet out in Arizona's Painted Desert, always next summer, never now.

pops.text: An album track from In My Tribe (1987) that became a quiet fan favorite without ever being a single.
Unusually, drummer Jerome Augustyniak shares the writing credit with Natalie Merchant on this one.
The Painted Desert is a real place — the colorful badlands of northeastern Arizona, part of the Petrified Forest region.
The song is built on postponement: the desert 'can wait till summer,' and so, painfully, can the reunion.
Peter Asher's production keeps it weightless — acoustic shimmer, Dennis Drew's keyboards, Merchant floating on top.
In My Tribe was the band's commercial breakthrough, spending well over a year on the Billboard album chart.
Merchant's writing here shows her signature move: a postcard-pretty image carrying a melancholy payload.
Decades later, keyboardist Dennis Drew was still revisiting the song at the piano for fans online.
The album version runs just under four minutes — a short story's worth of longing in a pop song's frame.

title: I Am A Man Of Constant Sorrow
description: A century-old folk lament reborn as a movie sensation — Dan Tyminski sings, George Clooney lip-syncs, and bluegrass conquers America.

pops.text: The song is traditional, first published by partially blind Kentucky fiddler Dick Burnett around 1913.
The Stanley Brothers' 1950 recording shaped the version most people know — Carter Stanley gets an arrangement credit here.
The Soggy Bottom Boys don't exist: they're the fictional band from the Coen brothers' O Brother, Where Art Thou?
That's Dan Tyminski of Alison Krauss's Union Station singing lead — George Clooney lip-syncs him on screen.
Producer T Bone Burnett built the film's soundtrack from pre-war American music, recorded live and raw.
The soundtrack won the Grammy for Album of the Year in 2002, beating U2 and Bob Dylan.
It sold millions of copies and kicked off a genuine bluegrass and Americana revival in the 2000s.
In the film, this is the song the escaped convicts cut at a backwoods radio station — and it makes them famous without them knowing.
The soundtrack album exists in multiple versions of this track, including the 'radio station' take and this full-band version.

title: Inn Town
description: Ryan Adams, barely out of his teens, opens Strangers Almanac with a slow, gorgeous shrug of a song about being broke and stuck in town.

pops.text: Opening track of Strangers Almanac (1997), the album that made Whiskeytown the great hope of alternative country.
Whiskeytown formed in Raleigh, North Carolina, in 1994 — Ryan Adams was still a teenager in its earliest days.
Adams was only about 22 when he recorded this album, but he'd already written a staggering pile of songs.
Caitlin Cary's violin and harmony vocals are the band's secret weapon all over this record.
Producer Jim Scott kept the sound warm and unhurried — this opener unspools at a strolling pace for nearly six minutes.
The lyric is pure small-town limbo: parking lots, cigarettes, and nowhere much to go.
The band was famously fractious — lineups churned and shows could be brilliant or shambolic, sometimes both.
Strangers Almanac got a deluxe reissue in 2008 stuffed with demos and outtakes from the sessions.
Adams disbanded Whiskeytown in 2000 and went solo; this album is the one fans hand to newcomers first.

title: Everything I Do
description: A country-soul slow burn from Strangers Almanac — every little thing the singer does just says he misses her.

pops.text: Track five on Strangers Almanac (1997) — sometimes listed with the subtitle '(Miss You)' after its refrain.
Guitarist Phil Wandscher opens it with swampy, curling lead lines that set the song's humid mood.
Ryan Adams wrote it; the whole lyric circles one admission — everything he does says 'I miss you.'
Caitlin Cary's fiddle and voice thread through the arrangement, pure Raleigh-meets-Nashville.
Whiskeytown were standard-bearers of the 'alt-country' wave that followed Uncle Tupelo's breakup.
The Strangers Almanac sessions were productive but tense; the band's classic lineup wouldn't last much longer.
Producer Jim Scott had worked with Tom Petty and the Rolling Stones — muscle memory shows in the roomy sound.
Adams reportedly wrote songs at a furious rate in this era, stockpiling material across several projects at once.
After Whiskeytown split in 2000, Adams launched a prolific solo career; Cary made acclaimed records of her own.

title: Astral Weeks
description: Van Morrison, 23 years old, walks into a New York studio with jazz musicians he's just met and conjures one of the most transcendent recordings ever made.

pops.text: Title track of Morrison's 1968 album, recorded in New York just a year after his pop hit 'Brown Eyed Girl.'
The backing band were top jazz session men: bassist Richard Davis, Modern Jazz Quartet drummer Connie Kay, guitarist Jay Berliner.
Producer Lewis Merenstein hired jazz players deliberately, betting their looseness would unlock Morrison's songs.
Morrison reportedly gave the musicians almost no direction — the tracks were largely captured in a handful of takes.
The album's sessions began on September 25, 1968, at Century Sound Studios; most of the record came fast.
It sold poorly on release and wasn't a hit anywhere — its reputation grew slowly, critic by critic.
Rolling Stone critic Lester Bangs wrote a famous essay calling the album a work of near-religious power.
The song's refrain — 'to be born again' — became the album's spiritual thesis in seven floating minutes.
Forty years later, in 2008, Morrison performed the whole album live at the Hollywood Bowl with Richard Davis back on bass.

title: Mustang Sally
description: A fictional Dublin soul band tears into Wilson Pickett's stomper — and a 17-year-old singer named Andrew Strong steals the whole movie.

pops.text: Mack Rice wrote the song; Wilson Pickett turned it into a No. 23 pop hit in 1966.
The 'ride, Sally, ride' chant traces back to the children's folk rhyme about Little Sally Walker.
The Commitments were a fictional band from Alan Parker's 1991 film, adapted from Roddy Doyle's novel.
Lead singer Andrew Strong was just 17 during filming — that gravelly soul voice startled everyone who heard it.
Director Alan Parker cast real musicians who could actually play, then filmed them like a working bar band.
The film's soundtrack album became a multi-million seller and briefly made Dublin soul a worldwide export.
In the story, this is the band's showstopper — the moment the rabble from Barrytown sounds like Memphis.
Strong's father was a singing coach who reportedly nudged his son toward the audition that changed his life.
Several cast members later toured as a real Commitments band, because audiences refused to let the fiction end.

title: Killing Me Softly With His Song
description: Roberta Flack hears a song on an airplane, reworks it at the piano, and turns it into a five-week No. 1 and a Grammy landmark.

pops.text: Writers Charles Fox and Norman Gimbel crafted it after singer Lori Lieberman described being transfixed by Don McLean in concert.
Lieberman recorded it first, in 1972 — her version is the one Flack heard playing on an airplane flight.
Flack reportedly worked out her arrangement on that flight and kept the song in reserve until the moment felt right.
Released in January 1973, it spent five weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100.
It won the 1974 Grammy for Record of the Year, plus Best Female Pop Vocal Performance for Flack.
The writers also took home Song of the Year — a clean sweep for a song about hearing a song.
Flack had won Record of the Year the year before too, for 'The First Time Ever I Saw Your Face' — the first artist ever to win it back-to-back.
Producer Joel Dorn kept the arrangement hushed: piano, soft rhythm section, and acres of space around her voice.
The Fugees revived it in 1996 with Lauryn Hill singing lead, introducing the song to a whole new generation.

title: Something To Talk About
description: A wink at the gossips: Raitt's slide guitar and Shirley Eikhard's long-shelved song finally give the neighbors exactly what they've been whispering about.

pops.text: Canadian songwriter Shirley Eikhard wrote this years before Raitt cut it — it had been passed on by other singers first.
It became the breakout single from Luck of the Draw (1991), Raitt's follow-up to her comeback album Nick of Time.
The single reached No. 5 on the Billboard Hot 100 — the biggest pop hit of Raitt's career.
It also won her the Grammy for Best Female Rock Vocal Performance.
Don Was produced the album, keeping her bottleneck slide guitar front and center.
Matt Mahurin directed the video: Raitt performs at a community gathering while older couples dance and swimmers fill a pool.
Raitt's resurgence was a decade in the making — she'd been dropped by her label in the mid-eighties before Nick of Time revived everything.
Luck of the Draw was dedicated to bluesman Stevie Ray Vaughan, who had died in 1990.
The album went multi-platinum and spent weeks near the top of the Billboard 200, peaking at No. 2.

title: The Obvious Child
description: A wall of Brazilian drums under a midlife meditation — Simon opens The Rhythm of the Saints thinking about age, sons, and the cross in the ballpark.

pops.text: Lead single from The Rhythm of the Saints (1990), Simon's follow-up to Graceland.
That thunderous drum track is Olodum, the Afro-Brazilian percussion collective from Salvador, Bahia.
Simon recorded the album's rhythm tracks in Brazil first, then wrote melodies and lyrics over them back home.
Olodum later brought the same thunder to Michael Jackson's 'They Don't Care About Us.'
The song reached No. 15 in the UK — Simon's strongest British solo showing in years.
The album topped the UK chart and reached No. 4 in the US, another world-music triumph after Graceland.
The lyric watches a boy named Sonny grow up and get married — Simon measuring his own life against the next generation.
Simon was pushing fifty and writing frankly about aging: 'I don't expect to be treated like a fool no more.'
The official video puts Olodum's drummers front and center — the beat is quite literally the star.

title: The City of New Orleans
description: Steve Goodman buys Arlo Guthrie a beer, plays him a train song, and folk history changes — the definitive ride down the Illinois Central line.

pops.text: Chicago songwriter Steve Goodman wrote it after riding the Illinois Central to visit family downstate.
Legend has it Goodman spotted Guthrie in a Chicago bar and bargained: one beer bought him the length of one song.
Guthrie's 1972 version, from his album Hobo's Lullaby, reached No. 18 on the Billboard Hot 100.
It was Guthrie's only Top 40 pop hit — not bad for the son of Woody Guthrie, who'd had his own train songs.
The train in the song was real: the City of New Orleans ran between Chicago and New Orleans for decades.
Amtrak kept the name alive, and the route still runs today — 'good morning, America, how are you?'
Willie Nelson's 1984 cover hit No. 1 on the country chart and won Goodman a songwriting Grammy, awarded after his death that same year.
Goodman died of leukemia in 1984 at just 36, but this song made him permanently part of American folk's furniture.
Guthrie kept singing it for fifty years — it became the song audiences would not let him leave the stage without.

title: Streets of Philadelphia
description: Springsteen walks Philadelphia's streets singing live into the cold for Jonathan Demme's AIDS drama — an Oscar, four Grammys, and his most haunted single.

pops.text: Director Jonathan Demme asked Springsteen for a song to open his 1993 film Philadelphia, one of the first major Hollywood films about AIDS.
Springsteen built it at home on synthesizer and drum machine, playing nearly everything himself.
The single reached No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100 — matching 'Dancing in the Dark' as his biggest pop hit.
It won the Academy Award for Best Original Song, over Neil Young's 'Philadelphia' from the same film.
At the 1995 Grammys it collected four awards, including Song of the Year and Best Rock Song.
Demme and his nephew Ted Demme directed the video on Philadelphia's actual streets.
For the video, Bruce sang live to a hidden microphone as he walked — that's a real location vocal, not a lip-sync.
Tom Hanks won his first Oscar starring in the film the song introduces.
Springsteen, the stadium bard of the working life, here sings for the people the city was learning not to look away from.

title: Sneakin' Sally Through The Alley
description: Before the suits and the MTV fame: a young English singer goes to New Orleans, hires the Meters, and cuts the funkiest debut of 1974.

pops.text: Title track of Palmer's 1974 solo debut, written by New Orleans master Allen Toussaint.
Toussaint had first given the song to Lee Dorsey, whose version appeared on his 1971 album Yes We Can.
Palmer recorded with members of the Meters — the funkiest backing band on Earth at that moment.
Little Feat's Lowell George also played on the album, linking two of the decade's great groove obsessives.
On the LP, this track arrives as the payoff of a seamless three-song suite with 'Sailing Shoes' and 'Hey Julia.'
Producer Steve Smith captured it all with a loose, second-line bounce straight out of New Orleans.
Palmer was a Yorkshireman who'd sung with soul band Vinegar Joe — the Crescent City was a pilgrimage, not a pose.
Ringo Starr covered the song three years later on Ringo the 4th.
Palmer's later MTV superstardom hid this chapter for years, but crate-diggers never stopped preaching this album.

title: Ride Like the Wind
description: Yacht rock at full gallop — a fugitive's midnight dash with Michael McDonald echoing the title and a guitar solo nobody expected from the quiet new guy.

pops.text: Lead single from Cross's 1979 debut album, released as a single in 1980.
It raced to No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100 and stayed there for four straight weeks.
That's Michael McDonald answering 'ride like the wind' in the background — the era's most valuable harmony voice.
Cross has cheerfully admitted he wrote the lyrics while tripping, on a drive from Houston to Austin.
The album was dedicated to Lowell George of Little Feat, who had died in 1979.
Producer Michael Omartian polished the record into the defining sound of early-eighties soft rock.
Cross played the stinging guitar solo himself — he was a serious player hiding inside a balladeer's image.
At the 1981 Grammys, Cross became the first artist to sweep the Big Four categories in a single night.
The song went 45 years without an official video until a brand-new clip arrived in 2025, directed by Andrea Calvetti.

title: Here's Where The Story Ends
description: Harriet Wheeler's feather-light voice over jangling guitars — the Sundays' dreamy signature, and the sound of 1990 indie pop at its most bittersweet.

pops.text: From the debut album Reading, Writing and Arithmetic, released in January 1990 on Rough Trade.
Singer Harriet Wheeler and guitarist David Gavurin met at the University of Bristol and wrote the band's songs together.
The single topped Billboard's Modern Rock Tracks chart in the US, an ocean away from their Bristol beginnings.
The video was shot outdoors in Berlin's Gendarmenmarkt, the band performing in the square beneath the French Cathedral.
Wheeler's voice — breathy, precise, slightly sad — became one of the most imitated sounds in nineties indie.
The album's title nods to the 'three Rs' of school, and its cover shows a fossil ammonite.
Dance act Tin Tin Out took the song back up the UK charts with a 1998 cover version.
The Sundays made only three albums, then quietly stepped away — Wheeler and Gavurin, by then married, raised a family.
Scarcity only burnished the legend: this remains one of the most beloved British singles of its era.

title: Can't Be Sure
description: The debut single that started it all — a young band on Rough Trade announcing, with total ambivalence, that they can't be sure about anything.

pops.text: The Sundays' debut single, released in 1989 on Rough Trade Records before the band had an album to its name.
It climbed to the top of the UK independent chart and made the British music press lose its collective mind.
Harriet Wheeler and David Gavurin formed the band after meeting at the University of Bristol.
The song shrugs beautifully: give her a story, give her a bed — certainty can wait.
Rough Trade boss Geoff Travis signed the band in the label's great post-Smiths era.
The single was re-recorded for the debut album Reading, Writing and Arithmetic, released in January 1990.
That album reached No. 4 in the UK — a remarkable landing for a first record on an independent label.
The video, shot for Geffen's US push, is all colored light and close-ups — Wheeler's face doing the storytelling.
Within a year of this single, the Sundays were the great hope of British guitar pop.

title: The Lighthouse's Tale
description: A lighthouse narrates its keeper's doomed love affair — three teenage virtuosos turn a ghost story into Nickel Creek's breakthrough ballad.

pops.text: From Nickel Creek's self-titled major-label debut (2000), produced by Alison Krauss.
The narrator is the lighthouse itself, watching its keeper fall for a sailor's wife — and it ends the way seaside ballads end.
Chris Thile was 19, Sara Watkins 18, and her brother Sean 23 when this album arrived; they'd already played together for a decade.
The trio met as kids at Southern California bluegrass festivals, where Thile and the Watkins siblings were contest-winning prodigies.
Released as a single in 2001, it reached No. 49 on Billboard's Hot Country Songs chart.
The video's lighthouse is the Cape Neddick Light — the famous 'Nubble' lighthouse off York, Maine.
The album went platinum, a startling feat for an acoustic trio with no drummer.
Krauss, a former child prodigy herself, was the perfect producer to polish virtuosity into emotion.
The song became their signature story-song — fans still request the sad lighthouse at every reunion show.

title: Reasons Why
description: Sean Watkins takes the lead on a clear-eyed breakup song — no villain, no drama, just a list of reasons that adds up to goodbye.

pops.text: From Why Should the Fire Die? (2005), the third Sugar Hill album by Nickel Creek.
Sean Watkins wrote it and sings lead — the guitarist stepping out from behind his sister Sara's spotlight.
Producer Eric Valentine, known for rock records, pushed the trio toward a darker, more dynamic sound.
The album debuted at No. 17 on the Billboard 200 and topped the bluegrass chart — their biggest commercial reach yet.
The lyric is an itemized heartbreak: not anger, just reasons, patiently stacked until leaving makes sense.
The official video is soft-focus and sunlit — the trio performing like the indie-pop band hiding inside the bluegrass one.
Two years after this album, Nickel Creek announced an indefinite hiatus that lasted until 2014's reunion album A Dotted Line.
Sara Watkins went on to solo records and I'm With Her; Chris Thile built Punch Brothers and took over hosting A Prairie Home Companion's successor, Live from Here.
In 2006 the song lent its name to the band's best-of collection, Reasons Why: The Very Best.

title: Overkill (Acoustic Version)
description: Men at Work's anxious 1983 hit, stripped to one guitar and one weathered voice — the acoustic remake that gave Colin Hay a second career.

pops.text: Colin Hay wrote the original for Men at Work's second album, Cargo (1983), in the white heat of sudden fame.
The Men at Work version reached No. 3 on the Billboard Hot 100.
It's a song about 3 a.m. anxiety — 'I can't get to sleep' — written by a man whose life had just exploded.
This acoustic remake anchors Hay's 2003 album Man @ Work, where he re-recorded his Men at Work catalog solo.
The title is a wink: the Men at Work frontman, literally a man at work, alone this time.
A year before the album, Hay performed the song wandering through a 2002 episode of Scrubs, guitar in hand, like J.D.'s personal Greek chorus.
Scrubs creator Bill Lawrence and star Zach Braff were devoted fans, and the cameo introduced Hay to a new generation.
Stripped down, Greg Ham's famous saxophone line disappears — and the melody turns out to need nothing at all.
Hay, born in Scotland and raised in Australia from age 14, still closes solo shows with this one, voice remarkably intact.

title: Down Under (Acoustic Version)
description: The land down under, unplugged: Hay revisits his and Ron Strykert's global anthem as a campfire singalong — Vegemite sandwich not included.

pops.text: Hay co-wrote the original with Men at Work guitarist Ron Strykert; it first appeared on Business as Usual in 1981.
The original spent four weeks at No. 1 in the US and also topped the UK chart — a rare double for an Australian band.
Greg Ham's flute riff later became the subject of a famous copyright case over its resemblance to the children's song 'Kookaburra.'
The lyric is a traveler's tall tale — a fried-out Kombi, a Vegemite sandwich, and locals who 'chunder' at the party.
It became Australia's unofficial anthem, blasted everywhere when Australia won the America's Cup in 1983.
This acoustic reading comes from Hay's Man @ Work project (2003), where he reclaimed his old hits one voice, one guitar.
The performance here is from Hay's own 'Song a Week' live series, filmed at San Francisco's Palace of Fine Arts.
In 2021, producer Luude's drum-and-bass remix with Hay's vocal stormed charts all over again, forty years on.
Hay has said the song began as a gentle joke about tourists — the world decided it was a national portrait instead.

title: Long Way Home
description: Waits and Kathleen Brennan write a hymn for the hopeless romantic who always takes the long way home — Norah Jones sang it first, then Tom reclaimed it.

pops.text: Waits wrote this with his wife and collaborator Kathleen Brennan — the partnership behind nearly all his work since the eighties.
They wrote it for Norah Jones, whose version appeared on her 2004 album Feels Like Home.
Waits' own recording surfaced on Orphans: Brawlers, Bawlers & Bastards (2006), his three-disc vault-clearing set.
It sits on the 'Bawlers' disc — Orphans sorts its songs into brawlers, bawlers and bastards, and this is pure bawler.
The lyric is a confession disguised as an apology: forgive me, pretty baby, but I always take the long way home.
Orphans gathered outtakes, soundtrack cuts and new recordings spanning two decades of Waits' career.
Where Jones made it smooth and moonlit, Waits makes it gravel and lamplight — same road, different traveler.
Brennan's influence is the tenderness: since Swordfishtrombones she's co-written the heart into his strangest records.
The set became one of the best-reviewed releases of Waits' career, proof the leftovers were main courses all along.

title: Hold On
description: Two people against a dying town, holding on by their fingertips — the plainspoken heart of Mule Variations and one of Waits' most beloved songs.

pops.text: From Mule Variations (1999), Waits' first studio album in six years and his debut for the independent ANTI- label.
Waits co-wrote it with Kathleen Brennan; they also produced the album together at Prairie Sun in Cotati, California.
The arrangement is nearly bare: Waits' voice, Marc Ribot's guitar, Larry Taylor's bass — nothing to hide behind.
The story follows a couple outlasting a town that's hanging up its sign and giving up.
The song earned Waits a Grammy nomination for Best Male Rock Vocal Performance.
Mule Variations itself won the Grammy for Best Contemporary Folk Album.
Matt Mahurin, who'd directed Waits videos before, shot the grainy, haunted clip for this one.
In 2013 the song closed a Walking Dead episode, sung by Beth Greene around the campfire — a whole new audience found it.
Waits recorded it in his late forties, and it sounds like it: not young hope, but the stubborn, seasoned kind.

title: One Little Song
description: A gentle, hopeful little meditation on the idea that somewhere out there is still one song nobody has ever sung.

pops.text: Welch sings this as a wish: somewhere there is still one little song that nobody has thought of yet.
It comes from Soul Journey (2003), her fourth album, named for the more searching, full-band turn her music took.
Soul Journey was Welch's first album to lean into drums and a fuller band sound instead of just two guitars.
Her partner David Rawlings co-produced the record, and his spidery, off-kilter guitar lines are all over it.
The album came out on Acony Records, the independent label Welch and Rawlings founded to release their own music.
Welch grew up in New York City and California, yet she writes and sings like an old Appalachian balladeer.
She and Rawlings met as students at Stanford University and have made nearly all their music together since.
Soul Journey also holds 'Look at Miss Ohio,' one of the most covered songs in Welch's catalog.
Never a single, 'One Little Song' became a quiet fan favorite — a songwriter's song about songwriting itself.

title: One More Dollar
description: A broke drifter's plea sung in a voice that sounds a hundred years old, from the debut album that helped launch the Americana revival.

pops.text: The narrator is down to his last luck and asking for one more dollar to get himself home.
This is from Revival (1996), Welch's debut album, produced by roots-music maestro T Bone Burnett.
Revival was nominated for the Grammy for Best Contemporary Folk Album.
Welch wrote the album's songs with David Rawlings, her lifelong musical partner.
The record was made in Nashville with a deliberately vintage approach, aiming for the feel of a lost 1930s disc.
Emmylou Harris recorded Welch's 'Orphan Girl' before Welch's own debut album was even out.
Revival's sepia-toned sound helped ignite the Americana boom that followed in the late 1990s.
Welch was only 28 when Revival was released, though the songs sound weathered far beyond her years.
Twenty years later she revisited these sessions on Boots No. 1, a collection of demos and alternate takes of this very song.

title: Just the Two of Us
description: The smoothest crossover ever cut: a jazz saxophonist, Bill Withers' warm baritone, and a groove that has never left the radio.

pops.text: Bill Withers co-wrote the song with William Salter and percussionist Ralph MacDonald.
It first appeared on Grover Washington Jr.'s album Winelight in 1980, then became a hit single in 1981.
The single reached No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100, a remarkable run for a jazz saxophonist.
It won the Grammy Award for Best R&B Song.
Early pressings of the single credited only Washington; Withers' featured billing was added on later pressings.
The session band was elite: Steve Gadd on drums and a young Marcus Miller on bass.
The full album version stretches past seven minutes; the hit single was edited down to about four.
Will Smith reworked the song in 1998 as a tribute to his young son, riding the same unmistakable groove.
More than four decades on, it remains the defining smooth-jazz crossover — equal parts romance and pure relaxation.

title: Nobody Told Me
description: Lennon's wry, bemused look at a strange world, recorded in 1980 and released after his death as one of his biggest solo hits.

pops.text: Lennon first sketched this idea back in 1976 under the working title 'Everybody's Talkin'.'
He recorded it during the 1980 sessions for Double Fantasy but left it off that album.
Lennon had originally considered giving the song to Ringo Starr for one of Ringo's solo albums.
It was released in January 1984 as the first single from the posthumous album Milk and Honey.
The single reached the Top 10 in both the United States and the United Kingdom.
Milk and Honey was planned as a companion piece to Double Fantasy, with songs traded between John and Yoko.
The promo video is a montage built largely from footage of Lennon and Yoko Ono's 1972 film Imagine.
Watch for cameos in the video: George Harrison, Andy Warhol, Fred Astaire and Miles Davis all flash by.
'Nobody told me there'd be days like these' became one of the most quoted lines of Lennon's whole solo career.

title: These Arms of Mine
description: A 21-year-old Otis Redding pleading over a slow Memphis groove — the record that started one of soul music's greatest careers.

pops.text: Redding wrote this song himself, a young singer's plea for somebody to hold.
It was his first single, released on Volt Records, a subsidiary of Memphis label Stax.
Redding had come to the studio as the driver and sometime singer for guitarist Johnny Jenkins' band.
When a Jenkins session ended early, Redding got the leftover studio time — and used it to cut this song.
Future Stax mainstay Steve Cropper played piano on the session.
The single became a modest R&B hit in 1963 and put Redding on the map.
It later opened his 1964 debut album, Pain in My Heart.
Redding was just 21 when he recorded it, but the ache in his voice already sounded lived-in.
The pleading, gospel-drenched ballad style he found here became the template for everything he did afterward.

title: Peg
description: Studio perfectionism at its funkiest — a bouncing groove, stacked Michael McDonald harmonies, and a guitar solo several legends failed to land.

pops.text: 'Peg' comes from Aja (1977), the album widely considered Steely Dan's studio masterpiece.
That wall of backing vocals answering the verses is Michael McDonald, layered over himself.
Walter Becker and Donald Fagen were by now studio-only perfectionists, hiring the best session players in Los Angeles.
Several top guitarists tried the solo and had their takes rejected before Jay Graydon nailed the famous one.
'Peg' reached No. 11 on the Billboard Hot 100, one of the band's biggest singles.
Aja won the Grammy Award for Best Engineered Album, a nod to how immaculate it sounds.
The crack band here includes drummer Rick Marotta driving that crisp, bouncing groove.
De La Soul sampled 'Peg' for their 1989 track 'Eye Know,' introducing the Dan to a hip-hop generation.
Fans have debated for decades who 'Peg' is about — Becker and Fagen, characteristically, never settled it.

title: Baby Come Back
description: Soft rock's ultimate apology: a pleading chorus so smooth it sailed to No. 1 and never really left the airwaves.

pops.text: Player's debut single, released in 1977, became one of the defining soft-rock hits of the decade.
Singer Peter Beckett wrote it with drummer J.C. Crowley, the band's two founding songwriters.
It climbed to No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 in January 1978 and stayed there for three weeks.
The song came from Player's self-titled debut album on RSO Records.
RSO was then the hottest label in pop, riding the Saturday Night Fever phenomenon.
Beckett, who was born in Liverpool, England, later built a long career writing songs for other artists and films.
The band formed in Los Angeles and honed this polished sound in the city's studio scene.
Decades later the song was embraced as a yacht-rock cornerstone, all satin harmonies and regret.
Its chorus has turned up in countless films, ads and TV shows — the universal soundtrack to 'take me back.'

title: Take Your Mama
description: A piano-pounding invitation to take your mother out dancing, from the glam-pop debut that ruled British pop in 2004.

pops.text: This opens Scissor Sisters' 2004 debut album and was released as one of its hit singles.
The premise is literal: take your mama out all night and show her a good time.
Jake Shears wrote it after taking his own mother out into New York nightlife and watching her light up.
The rollicking piano style channels Elton John, who became a friend of the band and later wrote with them.
The single reached the UK Top 20.
The band's debut became the best-selling album of 2004 in the United Kingdom.
Scissor Sisters formed in New York's queer club scene, mixing glam rock, disco and country kitsch.
Shears and Ana Matronic trade front-person duties across the album, a two-ring circus of a band.
It became the band's signature show-opener — a guaranteed way to get every generation in the room dancing.

title: I've Seen All Good People
description: A two-part suite that moves from a chess-game whisper to a full-throated rock chant — the record that saved Yes and launched prog's golden run.

pops.text: This is a two-part suite: the gentle 'Your Move' flowing into the rocking 'All Good People.'
It comes from The Yes Album (1971), the band's third record and their commercial breakthrough.
Jon Anderson wrote 'Your Move,' using a chess game as a metaphor for a relationship.
Listen to the backing vocals in 'Your Move' — they quietly quote John Lennon's 'Give Peace a Chance.'
An edited single version became Yes's first hit in America, reaching the Billboard Top 40.
The Yes Album was the first to feature guitarist Steve Howe, whose playing reshaped the band's sound.
The album genuinely saved the band: their label, Atlantic, had been close to dropping them.
The stacked a cappella harmonies in the second half became a template for the classic Yes sound.
From here Yes went straight into Fragile and Close to the Edge — prog rock's golden run started with this song.

title: Israelites
description: The record that carried reggae to the top of the British charts — a poor man's lament sung in rich Jamaican patois.

pops.text: Released in 1968, this became the first reggae song ever to top the UK singles chart, hitting No. 1 in 1969.
It was also a Top 10 hit in the United States, an astonishing first for Jamaican music.
Dekker co-wrote it and recorded it with his group the Aces for pioneering producer Leslie Kong.
The lyric compares the hardships of poor Jamaicans to the Israelites suffering in Egypt.
British listeners famously misheard the patois opening line about getting up in the morning to slave for bread.
Before this, Dekker was already a star at home in Jamaica, where singer Derrick Morgan had mentored him.
Leslie Kong's productions were slicker than most Jamaican records of the day, built to cross over.
The song charted in Britain all over again when it was reissued in the mid-1970s.
Years before Bob Marley's breakthrough, 'Israelites' opened the world's ears to reggae.

title: You Can Get It If You Really Want
description: Jimmy Cliff's can-do anthem in Dekker's hands — the perseverance sermon that became a UK smash and reggae's most quoted pep talk.

pops.text: The song was written by Jimmy Cliff, reggae's other great crossover star of the era.
Dekker's version reached No. 2 on the UK singles chart in 1970.
It was produced by Leslie Kong, the same man behind Dekker's 'Israelites' — and behind Cliff's early hits too.
Cliff recorded his own version, which reached the world in the landmark 1972 film The Harder They Come.
The lyric is a straight perseverance sermon: Rome was not built in a day, and opposition will come.
The track also titled Dekker's 1970 album, released during Trojan Records' British reggae boom.
Its loping rhythm catches Jamaican music mid-evolution, as ska was slowing down into reggae.
The song's message has made it a favorite far beyond reggae, quoted in speeches, ads and graduation halls.
Cliff and Dekker were friendly rivals — the two voices who first carried Jamaica onto British pop radio.

title: Finally Moving
description: Etta James's soul cry chopped over hip-hop drums — the track that announced Pretty Lights' free-music, electro-soul revolution.

pops.text: This comes from Taking Up Your Precious Time (2006), the debut album by Pretty Lights.
Pretty Lights is Derek Vincent Smith, a producer from Fort Collins, Colorado.
The track is built around a sample of Etta James's 1962 scorcher 'Something's Got a Hold on Me.'
Smith layered hip-hop beats under vintage soul samples and called the blend electro soul.
He gave his early albums away as free downloads, building a huge grassroots following before radio ever noticed.
Releasing on his own Pretty Lights Music label, he let fans pay what they wanted — or nothing at all.
That same Etta James vocal was later sampled by Avicii in his 2011 smash 'Levels.'
Smith's live shows became famous for their self-designed light rigs, as much a spectacle as the music.
'Finally Moving' stayed a centerpiece of his sets — the song where the whole crowd sings a 1962 soul sample.

title: Glycerine
description: One voice, one guitar and a cello: Gavin Rossdale's rain-soaked ballad about a love turning volatile, and Bush's most enduring song.

pops.text: 'Glycerine' was the fourth single from Bush's debut album, Sixteen Stone (1994).
Gavin Rossdale wrote it about a relationship coming apart — named for a substance that can turn explosive.
By Rossdale's own telling, the song came together quickly while he was living in London.
The arrangement is strikingly bare for a rock hit: just Rossdale's voice, his guitar and a cello.
It reached No. 1 on Billboard's Modern Rock Tracks chart.
The stark video, all spotlight and falling rain, put the entire focus on Rossdale's performance and became an MTV staple.
Sixteen Stone went on to sell more than six million copies in the United States alone.
Bush were a London band who, unusually, broke big in America long before Britain paid attention.
Three decades on, it remains their signature ballad — the quiet song that outlasted the loud ones.

title: Bitter Sweet Symphony
description: Richard Ashcroft walking straight through London and through life, over the most fought-over orchestral loop in rock history.

pops.text: The song is built on an orchestral loop sampled from the Andrew Oldham Orchestra's version of the Rolling Stones' 'The Last Time.'
It comes from Urban Hymns (1997), the album that made the Verve one of Britain's biggest bands.
The single reached No. 2 in the UK and broke the band in America, reaching the Billboard Top 20.
The sample triggered a famous legal fight: for over twenty years the songwriting royalties went to the Jagger-Richards camp.
In 2019, Mick Jagger and Keith Richards signed the rights back to Richard Ashcroft — a rare happy ending to a sampling saga.
Ashcroft's most quoted line sums up the song: you're a slave to money, then you die.
The iconic video, directed by Walter Stern, was filmed on Hoxton Street in east London.
In it Ashcroft walks in a straight line the whole song, barging past everyone and never breaking stride or expression.
The song was nominated for the Grammy for Best Rock Song and became Britpop's bittersweet closing anthem.

title: Let It Roll
description: New Orleans' brass-band ambassadors letting the sousaphone roll — street-parade energy from their Rounder Records album Unlock Your Mind.

pops.text: The Soul Rebels are an eight-piece brass band from New Orleans, formed in the early 1990s.
'Let It Roll' comes from their 2012 album Unlock Your Mind, released on the storied Rounder Records.
The band grew out of the city's young brass scene, inspired by the Dirty Dozen and Rebirth Brass Bands.
Their sound fuses second-line tradition with funk, soul and hip-hop — brass band music for a new century.
The album's title track features a guest appearance from New Orleans legend Cyril Neville.
That rolling bottom end is a sousaphone doing the job of a bass guitar, the brass band way.
The Rebels have shared stages with an unlikely range of stars, from Metallica to Nas.
This performance shows their calling card: call-and-response horns built to move a crowd down the street.
In New Orleans this music soundtracks second-line parades — the Rebels tour the world bringing that parade with them.

title: Wordless Chorus
description: Jim James dissolving into pure reverb and falsetto — the wordless wonder that opens Z, the album that carried My Morning Jacket to another level.

pops.text: This is the opening track of Z (2005), My Morning Jacket's fourth album.
True to its title, much of the song is literally wordless — James singing pure, soaring 'oohs.'
Z was produced by John Leckie, who had worked on Radiohead's The Bends.
It was recorded at Allaire Studios in the Catskills, a change from the band's home-studio beginnings.
Two new members joined for this album: guitarist Carl Broemel and keyboardist Bo Koster.
Jim James's voice is drenched in reverb — an echo he originally discovered singing in an empty grain silo.
The band formed in Louisville, Kentucky, James's hometown, in the late 1990s.
Z landed on critics' best-of-the-year lists in 2005 and is now routinely ranked among the finest albums of the 2000s.
Its slow, glowing build made 'Wordless Chorus' a signature concert opener for the band.

title: Girl, You'll Be a Woman Soon
description: Neil Diamond's pop plea turned slow and menacing for Pulp Fiction — the sound of Mia Wallace dancing toward trouble.

pops.text: Neil Diamond wrote this song and released the original in 1967, when it was a US Top 10 hit.
Urge Overkill recorded this version for Quentin Tarantino's Pulp Fiction (1994).
In the film it plays as Mia Wallace dances alone at Vincent's place — right before the night goes very wrong.
Tarantino famously scores his films by digging through his own record collection at home.
The Pulp Fiction soundtrack became a multi-million-selling phenomenon that revived several careers at once.
Where Diamond's original pleads, this version broods — slowed down into something moodier and more dangerous.
Urge Overkill, from Chicago, cultivated a lounge-lizard image, all matching suits and cocktail swagger.
The cover became the band's biggest hit, carried everywhere by the film's success.
Diamond reportedly loved the reinvention — his song had found a second life a generation later.

title: Go To the Mardi Gras
description: An English piano man in New Orleans opens his first live album with Professor Longhair's Mardi Gras anthem — and stretches it into something spooky and new.

pops.text: This is a Professor Longhair classic, first recorded around 1950 and long a Mardi Gras season standard.
It opens Mo Hippa Live (2008), Jon Cleary's first live album with the Absolute Monster Gentlemen.
Rather than charge in as a party song, Cleary's arrangement dances around the groove with spooky open spaces.
Cleary tweaked the lyric to 'going home to New Orleans,' giving the old song a post-Katrina ache.
Cleary was born in Cranbrook, England, but moved to New Orleans as a teenager and absorbed its piano tradition firsthand.
Before leading his own band, he spent years as the keyboard player in Bonnie Raitt's touring band.
Professor Longhair's rolling, rumba-tinged piano style is the foundation nearly all New Orleans R&B is built on.
The Absolute Monster Gentlemen are Cleary's longtime funk outfit, named with a wink at their polish.
Cleary later won a Grammy for his album Go Go Juice — not bad for a kid from Kent who followed the piano south.

title: Help Me Somebody
description: A deep soul plea stretched over nine minutes of New Orleans funk, and the vocal performance reviewers called the finest of Cleary's career to that point.

pops.text: This slow-burning soul plea comes from Mo Hippa Live (2008), recorded with the Absolute Monster Gentlemen.
Reviewers singled this track out as one of the strongest vocal performances Cleary had ever put on record.
Cleary plays piano in the direct lineage of Professor Longhair and Dr. John — rolling left hand, funky right.
He first arrived in New Orleans in the early 1980s, a teenage English blues fan who essentially never left.
His education was practical: years of club gigs, then a long stint as Bonnie Raitt's keyboardist.
Mo Hippa Live mixes Cleary originals with New Orleans standards like 'Tipitina,' played his own way.
The Gentlemen leave this groove wide open, letting the song smolder instead of boil.
The album's title nods to New Orleans slang and the city's own musical dialect, which Cleary speaks fluently.
His later album Go Go Juice won the Grammy for Best Regional Roots Music Album, sealing his adopted-hometown credentials.

title: Stir It Up
description: Marley's tender love song in its Catch a Fire form — the Wailers, all three original voices, introducing reggae to the rock world.

pops.text: Bob Marley wrote 'Stir It Up' as a love song, widely understood to be for his wife, Rita.
The Wailers first released it as a single back in 1967.
American singer Johnny Nash recorded it and scored a US hit with it in 1972.
Marley's own album version arrived on Catch a Fire (1973), the Wailers' debut for Island Records.
Island founder Chris Blackwell marketed the Wailers like a rock band — an album act, not a singles act.
The Jamaican recordings were overdubbed in London with rock guitar and keyboards to court rock audiences.
The first pressing of Catch a Fire came in a sleeve shaped like a Zippo lighter that flipped open.
This recording still features the original Wailers trio: Marley with Peter Tosh and Bunny Wailer.
'Stir It Up' became one of Marley's most covered songs, recorded by artists across soul, pop and country.

title: Trenchtown Rock
description: Live at London's Lyceum in 1975: Marley chanting for the Kingston neighborhood that raised him, on one of the greatest live reggae records ever made.

pops.text: This live version comes from Live! (1975), recorded at the Lyceum Theatre in London in July 1975.
The Lyceum concerts are widely ranked among the greatest live reggae performances ever captured.
The song celebrates Trenchtown, the Kingston neighborhood where Marley grew up in poverty.
Trenchtown produced an outsized share of Jamaica's music legends, from the Wailers onward.
Marley first recorded the song years earlier in sessions with producer Lee 'Scratch' Perry.
The same Live! album holds the famous concert version of 'No Woman, No Cry,' Marley's first UK hit.
Backing vocals come from the I Threes, including Rita Marley.
These 1975 London shows were pivotal in breaking reggae with British rock audiences.
Its chant-like chorus made 'Trenchtown Rock' a natural concert opener — one good thing about music, as the lyric says, is when it hits you feel no pain.

title: Lively Up Yourself
description: Marley's eternal warm-up call, stretched into a long groove live at the Roxy in 1976 as he was busy breaking America.

pops.text: The song first appeared on Natty Dread (1974), the first album billed to Bob Marley & The Wailers alone.
Peter Tosh and Bunny Wailer had left, so Natty Dread introduced the streamlined band heard here.
It became Marley's traditional concert opener — a warm-up call telling the crowd to liven up.
This version was recorded live at the Roxy Theatre in Los Angeles in 1976.
The Roxy show came on the Rastaman Vibration tour, the run that broke Marley in America.
Natty Dread also includes 'No Woman, No Cry' and 'Rebel Music (3 O'Clock Roadblock).'
The message is pure Marley uplift: liven up yourself, and don't be a drag.
The full Roxy concert was eventually released as the album Live at the Roxy in 2003.
Live, the tight studio track stretches into a long, rolling jam — exactly how Marley liked to start a night.

title: Jah Kingdom
description: Roots reggae at its most meditative: Burning Spear chanting Garvey's vision over a deep, unhurried groove.

pops.text: This is the title track of Burning Spear's 1991 album Jah Kingdom.
Burning Spear is Winston Rodney, a singer from St. Ann's Bay, Jamaica — the same parish that produced Bob Marley.
It was Marley himself who advised the young Rodney to take his music to Studio One in Kingston.
Rodney took his stage name from 'Burning Spear,' a title associated with Kenyan independence leader Jomo Kenyatta.
His music is devoted to the teachings of Marcus Garvey and the Rastafari faith.
His 1975 album Marcus Garvey is considered one of the greatest roots reggae records ever made.
Rodney's delivery — a chanting, meditative moan — is one of the most recognizable voices in reggae.
His albums were Grammy-nominated many times over, and he later won the reggae Grammy twice.
He is famous for marathon live shows with his Burning Band, turning concerts into something close to ceremony.

title: Wasting Time
description: The pro surfer turned songwriter drifting through a mellow groove about slowing down, from his Top 3 album On and On.

pops.text: 'Wasting Time' comes from On and On (2003), Jack Johnson's second album.
Johnson was a professional surfer first — at 17 he was the youngest surfer to reach the finals at Pipeline.
A serious wipeout at Pipeline, which cost him his front teeth, helped redirect him toward film and music.
On and On was produced by Mario Caldato Jr., best known for his work with the Beastie Boys.
It was recorded at Johnson's own Mango Tree Studio in Hawaii.
His rhythm section, drummer Adam Topol and bassist Merlo Podlewski, has backed him since the beginning.
The album reached No. 3 on the Billboard 200, confirming Johnson as surf-folk's laid-back king.
Johnson also co-founded the Kokua Hawaii Foundation, supporting environmental education in Hawaii's schools.
The song is a manifesto of sorts: in Johnson's world, wasting time well is never really wasted.

title: The Horizon Has Been Defeated
description: Evolution, physics and pirates of the new age, all delivered in Johnson's sunniest bounce — On and On's radio-ready single.

pops.text: Also from On and On (2003), this was released as one of the album's singles.
The lyric is unusually bookish for a beach song, mixing evolution and physics into its daydream.
Its title image — the horizon defeated by the pirates of the new age — is Johnson at his most poetic.
The track became a favorite on American triple-A and alternative radio.
Producer Mario Caldato Jr. brought a light hip-hop bounce he had honed with the Beastie Boys.
Johnson's career began almost by accident: G. Love recorded Johnson's song 'Rodeo Clowns' and put him on the map.
Many of the On and On songs were written on the road, touring behind his debut Brushfire Fairytales.
A few years later Johnson scored the Curious George film, carrying this sound to a generation of kids.
He and his wife Kim run the Johnson Ohana Foundation, funding music, art and environmental programs.

title: Jungle Love
description: A swaggering boogie-rock come-on from Book of Dreams, all strut, slide guitar and island-daydream lust.

pops.text: That opening guitar lick is pure strut — the band wanted a groove you could feel before a single word landed.
Surprise: Steve Miller didn't write this one. Guitarist Greg Douglass and bassist Lonnie Turner brought it to the band.
It's from Book of Dreams (1977), cut back-to-back with Fly Like an Eagle in the same marathon sessions.
Miller recorded so much material in that stretch that it filled two hit albums released within a year of each other.
The lyric's island fantasy — papayas, surf and rain — is peak 70s Miller: blues bones dressed in cosmic daydream.
Book of Dreams turned into a blockbuster, riding hits like Jet Airliner and Swingtown up the album charts.
That slippery lead guitar tone? Douglass was the band's secret weapon, adding a funkier edge than Miller's own playing.
The song became a classic-rock radio staple and a permanent fixture of Miller's live sets.
Decades on, it still sounds like summer — proof a great riff never needs much more than confidence.

title: Skin
description: A skittering, trance-like Ray of Light deep cut where Madonna whispers over William Orbit's jittery electronics.

pops.text: No video, no single — 'Skin' stayed a deep cut, which is exactly why fans treasure it.
Madonna wrote it with Patrick Leonard, her Like a Prayer partner, then handed it to producer William Orbit to mutate.
Orbit buried their classic pop songwriting under breakbeats, dub echoes and twitchy electronic pulses.
It sits on Ray of Light (1998), the album where Madonna swapped pop gloss for electronica and spiritual searching.
She'd recently trained vocally for Evita, and you can hear it — the singing is more controlled and breathy throughout.
The lyric keeps circling one question: do I know you from somewhere? Desire as déjà vu.
Ray of Light was recorded largely in Los Angeles, with Orbit building tracks from loops and hardware synths.
The album won multiple Grammys, including Best Pop Album, and critics called it Madonna's boldest reinvention.
A remix of 'Skin' finally surfaced officially in 2025 on the long-shelved companion project Veronica Electronica.

title: I Hear Music
description: Lady Day's 1940 bounce gets a Brooklyn lounge-groove rebuild on the Remixed & Reimagined project.

pops.text: Under the remix sits a master Billie Holiday recorded in September 1940 — her voice was barely 25 years old.
The song was written by Frank Loesser and Burton Lane for the 1940 film Dancing on a Dime.
This rebuild comes from Remixed & Reimagined (2007), where Legacy Records handed Holiday's Columbia masters to modern producers.
Remixers Swingsett and Takuya Nakamura re-cut it in Brooklyn, wrapping her vocal in a mid-tempo funk groove.
Takuya Nakamura is a trumpeter as well as a producer — listen for the plaintive horn lines answering Billie.
The project followed the same treatment given to Nina Simone a year earlier, proving jazz masters could fill dancefloors.
Holiday's phrasing is the remix's real instrument: she lags behind the beat like she's in no hurry at all.
Critics singled this opener out as one of the set's most faithful updates — groove added, dignity intact.
Seventy years between vocal take and remix, and she still sounds like the coolest person in the room.

title: Pennies from Heaven
description: Holiday's 1936 recording of the Depression-era standard, re-dressed in a London lounge remix.

pops.text: Billie's original master dates to November 19, 1936, cut with Teddy Wilson's orchestra when she was just 21.
The song came from the 1936 Bing Crosby film Pennies from Heaven, written by Arthur Johnston and Johnny Burke.
Its lyric was pure Depression comfort: don't waste the rain, because good fortune might fall with it.
Count De Money remixed this version at The Apartment in London for the 2007 Remixed & Reimagined album.
The remix keeps her feather-light vocal up front and slides a gentle club pulse underneath.
Holiday recorded for Columbia in this era, sessions that produced some of the finest small-group jazz ever made.
Teddy Wilson's piano was her perfect foil — elegant, swinging, and never stepping on her line.
The standard has been covered by everyone from Sinatra to Louis Armstrong, but Billie's lilt is unmistakable.
A song about luck falling from the sky, sung by a woman who made her own luck sound effortless.

title: Girl from the North Country
description: Dylan revisits his early ballad as a tender, crooning duet with Johnny Cash on Nashville Skyline.

pops.text: Dylan first released this song solo in 1963 on The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan. This duet take came six years later.
He re-recorded it with Johnny Cash in Nashville in February 1969, and it opens the Nashville Skyline album.
The melody borrows from the traditional ballad Scarborough Fair, which Dylan learned in London from Martin Carthy.
Cash and Dylan were mutual admirers — Cash had championed Dylan when much of Nashville still eyed him warily.
They cut more than a dozen songs together across two days; this is the only duet that made the album.
Dylan sings here in his smooth Nashville Skyline croon, a voice so changed that some fans didn't recognize him.
Weeks later the pair performed the song on the debut episode of The Johnny Cash Show, taped at the Ryman.
Producer Bob Johnston kept the arrangement bare — two voices, acoustic guitars, and a whole lot of respect.
Two American mythologies sharing one microphone, and neither one tries to out-sing the other.

title: I Don't Care Much
description: A Weimar-weary Cabaret standard turned dark-cabaret torch song by violinist-singer Emilie Autumn.

pops.text: This is a cover of a Kander and Ebb song from the 1966 Broadway musical Cabaret.
In the show it's sung by the Emcee — a shrug of a song about feeling nothing at all.
Autumn began violin at age four and trained classically before defecting to dark cabaret and industrial theatrics.
Her version slows the shrug into something sultry and bruised, with layered harmonies curling around the vocal.
It first appeared on her Chambermaid EP and was later collected on the rarities set A Bit o' This & That (2007).
Autumn built her world independently, releasing music through her own ventures and cultivating a devoted fanbase online.
She performs with an all-female backing troupe, The Bloody Crumpets, mixing burlesque, theatre and strings.
The lyric's trick: the singer insists she doesn't care — in a performance that cares enormously.
She later expanded her Victorian-asylum universe into a full autobiographical novel and stage musical.

title: Uncle Remus
description: Zappa and George Duke's gospel-tinged satire on race in America, hiding sharp teeth inside a sweet piano groove.

pops.text: Co-written with keyboard wizard George Duke, whose gospel-soaked piano carries the whole track.
It's from Apostrophe (') (1974), the album that became Zappa's first gold record in the US.
The title borrows Joel Chandler Harris's folk-tale narrator — Zappa aims the reference squarely at American racism.
Beneath the breezy groove, the lyric imagines fed-up Black Americans taking their frustrations out on Beverly Hills lawns.
Those lush backing vocals? Tina Turner and the Ikettes, recorded at Ike Turner's studio.
Tina reportedly loved the sessions; Ike, hearing the odd meters, was less enthusiastic about the invoice.
Apostrophe (') climbed to No. 10 on the Billboard 200 — Zappa's biggest album-chart success.
Duke later recut the song with a fuller gospel arrangement on his own album The Aura Will Prevail (1975).
Only Zappa could smuggle a civil-rights protest into a song this sunny. Listen again — the smile has an edge.

title: Bad Mouth
description: Two and a half minutes of DC post-hardcore impatience with people who talk instead of change.

pops.text: From Fugazi's debut EP, recorded in 1988 at Inner Ear Studios in Arlington, Virginia.
The band formed from the ashes of DC hardcore royalty — Ian MacKaye had fronted Minor Threat and Embrace.
Producer Ted Niceley and engineer Don Zientara kept it raw: this is a band in a room, barely contained.
The lyric is a dressing-down: you can't be what you were, so start being what you claim to be.
Guy Picciotto shares vocal duties across the EP, adding the band's signature call-and-response tension.
The EP came out on Dischord Records, the fiercely independent label MacKaye co-founded as a teenager.
In 1989 the EP was combined with Margin Walker to make the 13 Songs compilation most fans know.
Fugazi became famous for five-dollar, all-ages shows and refusing to play the major-label game.
Short, sharp and principled — 'Bad Mouth' is the sound of a band drawing its line in the sand.

title: The Killing Jar
description: A shimmering, urgent single from Peepshow, inspired by the butterfly collector's jar it takes its name from.

pops.text: Siouxsie said the song was inspired by how butterfly collectors use a killing jar to preserve a specimen's beauty.
It's the second single from Peepshow (1988), the album that finally broke the Banshees in America.
The band recorded Peepshow with new members and a poppier sheen, without sanding down their strangeness.
It reached No. 2 on Billboard's Modern Rock Tracks chart in the US, even as it peaked lower at home in the UK.
Producer Mike Hedges helped layer the track's chiming guitars and galloping momentum.
The video leans into the lepidoptera theme — the single's artwork wraps Siouxsie's face in morpho butterfly wings.
Peepshow's lead single Peek-a-Boo had just given them a US breakthrough; this kept the momentum running.
The extended 12-inch version was dubbed the Lepidopteristic Mix, because of course it was.
Beauty, capture and control in under four minutes — peak Banshees: gorgeous and slightly dangerous.

title: Sweet Tides
description: A blissed-out downtempo drift from Radio Retaliation, sung in French and English by Lou Lou Ghelichkhani.

pops.text: From Radio Retaliation (2008), Thievery Corporation's fifth studio album.
The vocal belongs to Lou Lou Ghelichkhani, the duo's longtime French-singing collaborator.
She drifts between French and English, which suits a song built like a slow tide coming in.
Rob Garza and Eric Hilton built Thievery in Washington, DC, bonding over bossa nova, dub and lounge records.
They founded their own label, Eighteenth Street Lounge Music, named after the DC club where they DJed.
Radio Retaliation wore its politics openly — its title track took aim at media and war.
This track is the album's exhale: strings, soft percussion and a melody that refuses to hurry.
Thievery record with a rotating cast of vocalists, which is why every album feels like a passport.
The duo later revisited the song in a symphonic setting, proving the drift works with an orchestra too.

title: Blue Orchid
description: A fuzz-blasted two-minute opener to Get Behind Me Satan, with a gothic video starring Karen Elson.

pops.text: The first single from Get Behind Me Satan (2005) — released barely six weeks after Jack White wrote it.
Basic tracking happened in March 2005 at Jack's own Third Man studio setup in Detroit.
That monstrous guitar sound is an Electro-Harmonix Big Muff pushed through an octave pedal. Two people, enormous noise.
It hit No. 43 on the Billboard Hot 100 and the UK top ten — huge reach for a two-minute fuzz blast.
Floria Sigismondi directed the video, a decaying-mansion fever dream in near-monochrome.
The woman in the video is model Karen Elson — she and Jack White married shortly after the shoot.
The clip ends with a horse rearing over Elson before cutting to black, and it landed on lists of the era's spookiest videos.
Rumors tied the lyric to a famous breakup; White denied it, and the mystery became part of the song's lore.
Get Behind Me Satan leaned on piano and marimba — but this opener is pure electric warning shot.

title: Little Ghost
description: A mandolin-led bluegrass romp about falling for a ghost only the singer can see.

pops.text: Yes, that's mandolin up front — Get Behind Me Satan traded garage fuzz for acoustic textures.
Jack White wrote the whole album's songs in roughly two weeks, chasing spontaneity over polish.
The lyric is a love song to a ghost: he's the only one who sees her, and he can't do much to please her.
The album was recorded at Third Man in Detroit in just a couple of weeks in early 2005.
Meg White's drumming stays deliciously minimal — the Stripes' whole aesthetic was built on restraint.
The record won the Grammy for Best Alternative Music Album, the band's second win in that category.
Live, the song became a showcase in the duo's From the Basement session, all creak and charm.
White has said the album's title nods to temptation — fitting for a record full of ghosts and devils.
Two minutes, one ghost, zero wasted notes. The sweetest haunting in the Stripes catalogue.

title: They Don't Dance Like Carmen No More
description: A wistful, funny tribute to Carmen Miranda from Buffett's first Key West-flavored album.

pops.text: From A White Sport Coat and a Pink Crustacean (1973), the album where Buffett found his tropical voice.
The Carmen in question is Carmen Miranda, the Brazilian star famous for fruit-laden hats and unstoppable rhumba energy.
Buffett wrote it as an old-timer's lament: the music got louder, but nobody dances like that anymore.
The album was recorded in Nashville with producer Don Gant, before Buffett's sound drifted fully beachward.
Its title spoofs Marty Robbins' A White Sport Coat (and a Pink Carnation) — Buffett humor from the start.
This was the record that introduced He Went to Paris, now one of his most beloved story songs.
Buffett had just washed up in Key West after his Nashville country career stalled — the best failure of his life.
The track stayed a fan-favorite deep cut, turning up in live sets for decades, including a rowdy 1974 Sausalito session.
Ten cents a dance, he sighs at the end. Some bargains really are gone forever.

title: A Pirate Looks at Forty
description: Buffett's defining ballad — a smuggler born centuries too late, watching the ocean and doing the math on his life.

pops.text: Buffett wrote it about Phil Clark, a real Key West character — smuggler, mercenary, and fixture of the Chart Room bar.
It's from A1A (1974), named for the coastal highway running down Florida's Atlantic edge.
The song never mentions Margaritaville-style partying; it's a midlife confession set to a gentle waltz of regret.
Released as a single in 1975, it only bubbled under the Hot 100 — its legend grew entirely through live shows.
For the radio single, a verse was trimmed. The full album version is the one fans guard jealously.
Buffett later titled his memoir A Pirate Looks at Fifty, checking back in on the song a decade on.
Jack Johnson, Dave Matthews and Bob Dylan have all covered or performed it — songwriters recognize a standard.
After Buffett's death in 2023, Dave Matthews Band opened their next show with it in tribute.
Mother, mother ocean: the chorus every Parrot Head can sing with their eyes closed and their heart open.

title: Nautical Wheelers
description: A drunken, affectionate portrait of Key West's square-dancing misfits, closing out A1A's magical second side.

pops.text: The Nautical Wheelers were a real Key West square-dance group Buffett used to watch in the 1970s.
The song sits on A1A (1974), the album fans often call his finest — Pirate Looks at Forty lives here too.
Buffett paints Duval Street as a carnival of artists, smugglers and beautiful losers, and counts himself among them.
It was recorded in Nashville with producer Don Gant, though its soul is entirely Key West.
The gentle, tipsy sway of the arrangement mirrors a night drifting from bar to dance floor and back.
A1A's second side is stacked: this, Tin Cup Chalice and Pirate form a holy trinity for deep-cut fans.
Buffett kept the song in live sets for fifty years, often as a breather between the big party anthems.
A live version anchored his Tales from MargaritaVision video collection, introduced by Buffett himself.
Proof that his best writing was never just about beaches — it's about the glorious oddballs who gather near them.

title: Sweet Caroline
description: Denver honky-tonkers the Railbenders give Neil Diamond's singalong a bar-band country kick, live at Herman's Hideaway.

pops.text: The song is Neil Diamond's 1969 classic — the Railbenders cut their studio version on their 2003 album Segundo.
The Railbenders are a Denver alternative-country outfit, formed in the late 1990s bar scene.
This performance was filmed at Herman's Hideaway, a storied Denver rock club on South Broadway.
Diamond has told shifting stories about the title — most famously linking it to a photo of young Caroline Kennedy.
The crowd's bah-bah-bah and so-good responses weren't in Diamond's recording; audiences invented them over decades.
Boston's Fenway Park adopted the song in the late 1990s, turning it into an eighth-inning ritual.
A Denver band leading a Boston anthem in a packed bar — and the Colorado crowd knows every response anyway.
Diamond's original reached No. 4 on the Billboard Hot 100 and became his signature live closer.
Some songs become folk music by sheer repetition. This is one, in any accent you sing it.

title: Cry Little Sister
description: The Lost Boys' gothic theme — Gerard McMann's haunted plea floating over Michael Mainieri's synth mist.

pops.text: Written for The Lost Boys (1987) by Gerard McMann — real name Gerard McMahon — with producer Michael Mainieri.
Remarkably, they wrote it before seeing a single frame of the film. It never mentions vampires at all.
McMann later worked under the name G Tom Mac, and the song became his signature by a mile.
The children's-choir chant of thou shalt not fall gives the track its delicious church-meets-crypt chill.
The Lost Boys soundtrack is a cult object itself, featuring INXS, Lou Gramm and Echo & the Bunnymen covering the Doors.
Director Joel Schumacher's film made teen vampires cool; this song made them sound eternal.
The track never charted big on release — its fame grew with the film's endless cable and Halloween afterlife.
Marilyn Manson covered it in 2018, introducing the sister to a whole new generation of night owls.
Cry, little sister: the rare movie theme that out-haunts the movie.

title: Lola
description: Ray Davies' Soho encounter set to an irresistible singalong — the Kinks' comeback hit with a famous lyrical twist.

pops.text: Ray Davies based it on a story about the band's manager dancing all night with someone not quite who he assumed.
The BBC balked at the words Coca-Cola as product placement, so Davies flew back mid-tour to re-sing it as cherry cola.
That transatlantic dash to fix two words worked: Lola hit No. 2 in the UK and the US top ten in 1970.
It rescued the Kinks commercially after years banned from touring America had stalled their momentum.
The song opens the concept album Lola Versus Powerman and the Moneygoround, a satire of the music business.
That warm acoustic strum and the National steel resonator give it its unmistakable front-porch glow.
Davies has always called it a love song, and its gentle, unbothered tone was radical for 1970 radio.
The official animated video arrived 50 years later, in 2020, retelling the Soho night as a comic book.
L-O-L-A: four letters, one raised eyebrow, and a chorus nobody has ever sung quietly.

title: I Love You Always Forever
description: A Welsh singer's feather-light debut single that floated at No. 2 for nine weeks in the summer of 1996.

pops.text: Welsh singer Donna Lewis wrote and performed it for her debut album Now in a Minute (1996).
It spent nine weeks at No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100 — kept from the top by Los del Río's Macarena.
On the Hot 100 Airplay chart it did reach No. 1, because radio simply would not stop playing it.
Lewis trained as a classical pianist and flautist and studied music in Cardiff before going pop.
That whispered, layered vocal was her signature — she stacked her own harmonies into a soft cloud.
The title phrase nods to a Welsh folk-song tradition of pledging love in absolutes.
The video keeps it simple: Lewis at a piano in sunlit gauze, matching the song's weightless feel.
It became a global hit, topping charts in several countries and defining summer 1996 for slow dancers.
Lewis later re-recorded it decades on — the voice, remarkably, sounds just as feather-light.

title: Grey Cell Green
description: Stourbridge grebo heroes and their two-bass attack, riding God Fodder's catchiest chorus.

pops.text: Spot the trick: Ned's Atomic Dustbin had TWO bass players, Alex Griffin and Mat Cheslin, splitting high and low parts.
From God Fodder (1991), the Stourbridge band's debut album, a cornerstone of the British grebo scene.
The band took their name from a 1959 episode title of The Goon Show. British silliness, serious riffs.
God Fodder cracked the UK top five — a remarkable landing for a band in baggy shorts playing this fast.
The song became a US college-radio and 120 Minutes staple, their calling card across the Atlantic.
Singer Jonn Penney's delivery rides the twin-bass churn like a surfer who knows the wave personally.
The band's T-shirts were inescapable in early-90s Britain; their merch game rivaled their gig game.
They recorded for Columbia in the US after indie success on their own Furtive label at home.
Two basses should be a gimmick. On this track it's an engine — and it still sounds enormous.

title: The Wind
description: Ninety seconds of pure stillness opening Teaser and the Firecat — Stevens listening to where his soul leads.

pops.text: It's barely a minute and three quarters long, and it opens Teaser and the Firecat (1971) like a held breath.
Stevens wrote it as a small spiritual compass: he listens to the wind, and to where his soul says to go.
The album hit No. 2 in both the UK and US and made him a full-blown superstar at 23.
Producer Paul Samwell-Smith, formerly of the Yardbirds, kept the arrangement to little more than voice and guitar.
Decades later Wes Anderson placed the song in Rushmore, handing it to a new generation in one perfect scene.
It also turns up in Almost Famous, Cameron Crowe's love letter to this exact era of music.
Stevens painted the album's whimsical cover art himself — the Teaser and the Firecat were his own characters.
He'd later step away from pop fame entirely, returning to music as Yusuf after a long spiritual detour.
The shortest song in this sprint, and maybe the one that lingers longest.

title: Love of the Common People
description: Paul Young's warm reggae-pop cover of the Hurley and Wilkins standard, a UK No. 2 from No Parlez.

pops.text: Written by John Hurley and Ronnie Wilkins in 1967, it was recorded by the Four Preps and the Everly Brothers before Young.
Nicky Thomas's reggae version was a UK hit in 1970 — Young's take borrows that Caribbean warmth.
It's from No Parlez (1983), the debut album that made Paul Young one of Britain's biggest new voices.
The single reached No. 2 on the UK chart, held off the top at the height of his breakthrough run.
His version nearly stalled early in its chart life, then climbed back — a slow-burn hit story.
The lyric is no fairy tale: it's about poverty, pride and a family's love holding the roof up.
Young's soulful ache was the selling point — a blue-eyed soul voice compared early on to Marvin Gaye's warmth.
No Parlez also carried his chart-topping cover of Wherever I Lay My Hat, Gaye's own song.
A song about having little but love, sung like it's the richest thing in the world.
